## What Is Chapter 7 in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/chapter-7.html

What Is Chapter 7 in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Chapter 7

Chapter 7 is the most common form of bankruptcy, often called liquidation bankruptcy. The trustee sells the debtor's non-exempt property to pay creditors, and most remaining unsecured debts are discharged. The process typically takes 3 to 6 months from filing to discharge.

How It Works

Chapter 7 bankruptcy provides a fresh start by eliminating most unsecured debts - credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, and old utility bills. The debtor must pass the means test (or have income below the state median) to qualify. After filing, the trustee reviews assets, conducts the 341 meeting, and determines whether any non-exempt property exists to liquidate.

In practice, approximately 95% of Chapter 7 cases are 'no-asset' cases, meaning the trustee finds no property worth liquidating. The debtor keeps all exempt property - typically a home (up to the homestead exemption), a vehicle (up to the motor vehicle exemption), retirement accounts, and personal belongings.

The Chapter 7 discharge is typically entered about 60 days after the 341 meeting, roughly 4 months after filing. The discharge permanently eliminates the debtor's personal liability on dischargeable debts. Secured debts survive unless the debtor surrenders the collateral, redeems it, or reaffirms the debt.

Key Facts

Most common bankruptcy chapter - over 60% of all consumer filings

Requires passing the means test or having below-median income

About 95% of cases are 'no-asset' - the debtor keeps all property

Discharge entered approximately 60 days after the 341 meeting

Cannot file Chapter 7 again for 8 years after a prior Chapter 7 discharge

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Chapter 7 Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

What debts does Chapter 7 eliminate?

Chapter 7 eliminates most unsecured debts: credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, past-due utilities, and many lawsuit judgments. It does not eliminate student loans (usually), recent taxes, child support, alimony, or debts from fraud.

Will I lose my house in Chapter 7?

Not necessarily. If your home equity is within your state's homestead exemption and you stay current on mortgage payments, you can keep your home. The trustee will only sell your home if it has significant non-exempt equity.

How long does Chapter 7 stay on my credit report?

A Chapter 7 bankruptcy remains on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. However, most people see significant credit score improvement within 12-18 months of discharge.

Related Terms

Means Test
Discharge
Liquidation
Chapter 13

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Claim in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/claim.html

What Is Claim in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Claim

A claim in bankruptcy is a creditor's right to payment from the debtor or the bankruptcy estate. Claims are classified as secured, unsecured priority, or general unsecured, and the classification determines the order and amount of payment the creditor receives in the bankruptcy case.

How It Works

Creditors assert claims by filing a proof of claim form with the bankruptcy court. The claim must include the amount owed, the basis for the claim, and any supporting documentation. In Chapter 7 no-asset cases, creditors are not required to file proofs of claim because there is nothing to distribute.

Claims are classified into three main categories. Secured claims are backed by collateral (mortgages, car loans) and are paid first from the collateral's value. Priority claims (taxes, domestic support obligations, administrative expenses) are paid before general unsecured claims. General unsecured claims (credit cards, medical bills) are paid last and often receive only pennies on the dollar.

The debtor or trustee can object to a claim if the amount is wrong, the claim is untimely, or the claim is otherwise invalid. Disputed claims are resolved by the bankruptcy court. The bar date - the deadline for filing proofs of claim - is set by the court and strictly enforced.

Key Facts

Filed on Official Form 410 (Proof of Claim) with supporting documentation

Three main types: secured, priority unsecured, and general unsecured

The bar date is the deadline for filing - late claims may be disallowed

The debtor or trustee can object to any claim

In Chapter 7 no-asset cases, claims do not need to be filed

Frequently Asked Questions

What if a creditor does not file a claim?

If a creditor does not file a proof of claim by the bar date, the claim may be disallowed and the creditor receives nothing from the estate. In Chapter 13, the debtor can file a claim on behalf of the creditor.

Can I dispute a creditor's claim?

Yes. You can file an objection to a claim if the amount is incorrect, the debt is not owed, or the claim was filed late. The court will schedule a hearing to resolve the objection.

What is the difference between a claim and a debt?

All debts are potential claims, but a claim specifically refers to the formal assertion of a right to payment in the bankruptcy case. A debt becomes a claim when the creditor files a proof of claim or the debt is scheduled by the debtor.

Related Terms

Proof of Claim
Secured Claim
Unsecured Claim
Priority Claim

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Confirmation in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/confirmation.html

What Is Confirmation in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Confirmation

Confirmation is the court's approval of a Chapter 11 or Chapter 13 repayment plan, making the plan legally binding on the debtor and all creditors. Once confirmed, the plan governs the rights and obligations of all parties for the duration of the case.

How It Works

In Chapter 13, the debtor proposes a plan and the court holds a confirmation hearing, typically 20-45 days after the 341 meeting. The court evaluates whether the plan meets all statutory requirements: good faith, best interests test, feasibility, payment of priority claims in full, and commitment of all disposable income (for above-median debtors).

Creditors and the trustee can object to confirmation. Common objections include: the plan is not feasible, the debtor is not committing all disposable income, the plan was not proposed in good faith, or the plan fails the best interests test. The debtor can modify the plan to address objections.

In Chapter 11, confirmation is more complex. The debtor files a disclosure statement and plan, creditors vote on the plan by class, and the court evaluates whether the plan meets the requirements of Section 1129. A plan can be confirmed consensually (all impaired classes accept) or through cram down (over the objection of some classes).

Key Facts

Makes the plan legally binding on the debtor and all creditors

Chapter 13 requirements: good faith, feasibility, best interests, disposable income

Chapter 11 requires creditor voting and a disclosure statement

The trustee and creditors can object to plan confirmation

Post-confirmation modifications are possible but require court approval

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Plan Confirmation

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if my plan is not confirmed?

The court may allow you to modify the plan and try again. If the plan cannot be modified to meet requirements, the case may be dismissed or converted to Chapter 7.

Can the plan be changed after confirmation?

Yes. Both the debtor and the trustee can request a plan modification after confirmation if circumstances change - job loss, medical emergency, or changed financial circumstances.

How long does confirmation take?

In Chapter 13, confirmation typically occurs within 2-3 months of filing. In Chapter 11, the process is longer - often 6-18 months depending on the complexity of the case and creditor negotiations.

Related Terms

Chapter 13
Best Interests Test
Feasibility
Good Faith

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Cram Down in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/cram-down.html

What Is Cram Down in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Cram Down

A cram down allows a bankruptcy court to confirm a reorganization plan over the objection of one or more classes of creditors, provided the plan meets specific statutory requirements. In Chapter 13, it also refers to reducing a secured claim to the collateral's current value.

How It Works

In Chapter 13, the term 'cram down' commonly refers to reducing the amount owed on a secured debt to the current value of the collateral. If a debtor owes $15,000 on a car worth $9,000, the court can 'cram down' the secured claim to $9,000, with the remaining $6,000 treated as unsecured debt. This requires that the loan be more than 910 days old for vehicles (the 'hanging paragraph').

In Chapter 11, cram down is the mechanism for confirming a plan over the objection of a dissenting class of creditors under Section 1129(b). The plan must be 'fair and equitable' and must not 'discriminate unfairly' against the dissenting class. For secured creditors, fair and equitable means retaining liens and receiving the present value of the collateral.

The interest rate applied in a cram down is determined by the 'prime plus' approach established in Till v. SCS Credit Corp. (2004). The court starts with the prime rate and adds a risk adjustment, typically 1-3%, based on the circumstances of the case.

Key Facts

Chapter 13 vehicle cram down requires the loan to be more than 910 days old

Reduces secured claim to current value of collateral

Chapter 11 cram down requires the plan to be 'fair and equitable'

Interest rate set using 'prime plus' approach (Till v. SCS Credit Corp.)

The 'hanging paragraph' (910-day rule) prevents cram down on recent vehicle loans

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Cram Down Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I cram down my mortgage?

Generally no. Section 1322(b)(2) prohibits modifying a mortgage secured only by the debtor's principal residence. However, if the mortgage also secures other property, modification may be possible. Second mortgages can be stripped in some circuits if the home is underwater.

What is the 910-day rule?

The 910-day rule (BAPCPA's 'hanging paragraph') prevents cram down on vehicle loans incurred within 910 days (about 2.5 years) before filing. For these recent loans, the debtor must pay the full contract balance, not just the vehicle's current value.

How is the cram down interest rate calculated?

Courts typically use the 'prime plus' formula from Till v. SCS Credit Corp.: start with the national prime rate and add 1-3% for risk. The total rate is usually lower than the original contract rate.

Related Terms

Secured Claim
Confirmation
Chapter 13
Lien Stripping

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Current Monthly Income in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/current-monthly-income.html

What Is Current Monthly Income in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Current Monthly Income

Current monthly income (CMI) is a defined term in bankruptcy law meaning the debtor's average monthly gross income from all sources over the six full calendar months before the bankruptcy filing date. It is used to determine whether the debtor is above or below median income for means test purposes.

How It Works

CMI is calculated by adding all gross income from all sources received during the six complete calendar months before filing, then dividing by six. For example, if filing in July, the calculation uses income from January through June. This includes wages, salary, commissions, bonuses, overtime, business income, rental income, pension, and contributions from others.

Certain income sources are excluded from CMI: Social Security benefits, payments to victims of war crimes or terrorism, and VA disability benefits. These exclusions can significantly help debtors who rely on these income sources qualify for Chapter 7.

CMI is reported on Form 122A-1 (Chapter 7) or Form 122C-1 (Chapter 13). The annualized CMI is compared to the state median for the debtor's household size. If below median, the debtor passes the means test. If above, the debtor must complete the full means test calculation.

Key Facts

Defined at 11 U.S.C. Section 101(10A)

Based on 6 full calendar months before the filing month (not the filing date)

Includes almost all income: wages, business, rental, pension, and third-party contributions

Social Security and VA disability benefits are excluded

Reported on Form 122A-1 (Chapter 7) or Form 122C-1 (Chapter 13)

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Means Test Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does bankruptcy use a 6-month average instead of current income?

Congress designed the means test to look at the debtor's recent earnings history, not just a single month's income. This prevents debtors from strategically timing their filing to take advantage of a temporarily low-income month.

Does my spouse's income count?

If you are married and filing individually, your spouse's income is included in the household CMI calculation on Form 122A-1 but can be offset by a 'marital adjustment' for the spouse's separate expenses on Form 122A-2.

Can I time my filing to lower my CMI?

Yes, strategic timing is common. If you received a large bonus, overtime, or settlement in a recent month, waiting until that month drops out of the 6-month window can lower your CMI and help you pass the means test.

Related Terms

Above Median Income
Means Test
Disposable Income
Chapter 7

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Debtor in Possession in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/debtor-in-possession.html

What Is Debtor in Possession in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Debtor in Possession

A debtor in possession (DIP) is a debtor in a Chapter 11 bankruptcy case who retains control of their assets and continues to operate their business under court supervision. The DIP has most of the powers and duties of a trustee, including the duty of loyalty to creditors.

How It Works

In Chapter 11, the debtor automatically becomes the debtor in possession when the case is filed. Unlike Chapter 7, no trustee is appointed to take over the business. The DIP continues to manage day-to-day operations, pay employees, serve customers, and run the business in the ordinary course.

The DIP has enhanced obligations compared to operating outside of bankruptcy. The DIP must file monthly operating reports with the court, maintain adequate insurance, pay post-petition taxes, and operate in the best interests of creditors. The DIP cannot make extraordinary transactions (selling assets outside the ordinary course, obtaining new financing) without court approval.

If the DIP engages in fraud, dishonesty, incompetence, or gross mismanagement, the court can appoint a Chapter 11 trustee to replace the DIP. This is relatively rare - courts prefer to leave the debtor in control when possible, especially in small business cases under Subchapter V.

Key Facts

The debtor automatically becomes DIP upon Chapter 11 filing - no appointment needed

Has most powers and duties of a trustee under 11 U.S.C. Section 1107

Must file monthly operating reports and maintain insurance

Can operate in the ordinary course without court approval

A Chapter 11 trustee replaces the DIP only for cause (fraud, mismanagement)

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the DIP borrow money?

Yes, but obtaining new financing (DIP financing) requires court approval under Section 364. DIP lenders often receive super-priority administrative expense status or liens on estate property, making DIP financing expensive.

What is the difference between a DIP and a trustee?

A DIP is the debtor managing its own affairs. A trustee is a court-appointed outsider who replaces management. In most Chapter 11 cases, the debtor remains as DIP. A trustee is appointed only in rare cases involving fraud or gross mismanagement.

Does the DIP concept apply in Chapter 13?

Not formally. Chapter 13 debtors keep possession of their property but do not hold the legal title of 'debtor in possession.' The concept is specific to Chapter 11.

Related Terms

Chapter 11
Case Trustee
Confirmation
Adequate Protection

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Discharge Injunction in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/discharge-injunction.html

What Is Discharge Injunction in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Discharge Injunction

The discharge injunction is a permanent court order under 11 U.S.C. Section 524(a) that prohibits any act to collect, recover, or offset a discharged debt. It protects the debtor's fresh start by making it illegal for creditors to pursue collection on eliminated debts after the bankruptcy case concludes.

How It Works

When the court enters a discharge order, the discharge injunction takes effect automatically. It prohibits creditors from initiating or continuing any action to collect a discharged debt, including lawsuits, phone calls, letters, wage garnishments, and credit reporting of the debt as currently owing.

The discharge injunction is permanent and applies to the debtor personally. However, it does not protect co-debtors (except in Chapter 13, where the co-debtor stay provides limited protection during the plan). It also does not prevent enforcement of valid liens - a creditor can still foreclose on a house or repossess a car if payments are not made.

Violations of the discharge injunction can be addressed through a contempt motion. Courts can award actual damages, attorney fees, and in egregious cases, punitive damages. Some circuits treat discharge injunction violations under Section 524 while others apply Section 105(a) contempt powers.

Key Facts

Codified at 11 U.S.C. Section 524(a)

Prohibits any act to collect a discharged debt - permanently

Violations can result in contempt, damages, and attorney fees

Does not remove liens - only eliminates personal liability

Does not protect co-debtors (except the Chapter 13 co-debtor stay)

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: 524 Injunction Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

What should I do if a creditor contacts me about a discharged debt?

Notify the creditor in writing that the debt was discharged, provide a copy of the discharge order, and demand they cease collection. If they continue, consult a bankruptcy attorney about filing a contempt motion - you may be entitled to damages.

Does the discharge injunction stop credit reporting?

Yes. Creditors must report discharged debts as 'discharged in bankruptcy' with a zero balance. Reporting a discharged debt as owing or delinquent violates the discharge injunction.

How long does the discharge injunction last?

The discharge injunction is permanent. There is no expiration date. Even after the bankruptcy is removed from your credit report (10 years for Chapter 7, 7 years for Chapter 13), the discharge injunction remains in effect forever.

Related Terms

Discharge
Automatic Stay
Stay Violation
Fresh Start

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Discharge in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/discharge.html

What Is Discharge in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Discharge

A discharge is a court order that permanently eliminates the debtor's personal liability for specified debts, prohibiting creditors from ever attempting to collect those debts. It is the primary goal of most individual bankruptcy filings and provides the 'fresh start' that bankruptcy law is designed to give.

How It Works

The discharge is the culmination of the bankruptcy process. In Chapter 7, the discharge is typically entered about 60 days after the 341 meeting - roughly 4 months after filing. In Chapter 13, the discharge is entered after the debtor completes all plan payments, which takes 3-5 years.

The discharge operates as a permanent injunction under 11 U.S.C. Section 524(a). Any creditor who attempts to collect a discharged debt - including phone calls, letters, lawsuits, or reporting the debt as owing on credit reports - violates the discharge injunction and can be held in contempt of court.

Not all debts are dischargeable. Certain debts survive bankruptcy, including most student loans, recent tax obligations, child support and alimony, debts from fraud, DUI-related debts, and certain government fines. The categories of non-dischargeable debts are listed in 11 U.S.C. Section 523.

Key Facts

Permanently eliminates personal liability for dischargeable debts

Chapter 7 discharge: approximately 60 days after the 341 meeting

Chapter 13 discharge: after completing all plan payments (3-5 years)

Operates as a permanent injunction under Section 524(a)

Some debts (student loans, recent taxes, support obligations) survive discharge

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Discharge Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Does discharge eliminate liens?

No. A discharge eliminates personal liability but does not remove liens. A creditor with a mortgage lien can still foreclose if payments are not made, even though the debtor's personal liability on the note is discharged.

Can a discharge be revoked?

Yes, in limited circumstances. Under Section 727(d), a discharge can be revoked within one year if the debtor obtained it through fraud, failed to disclose property, or refused to obey a court order.

What is the difference between Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 discharge?

Chapter 13 historically offered a broader discharge (called a 'super discharge'), but BAPCPA narrowed this advantage significantly. The main differences now are timing (4 months vs. 3-5 years) and the fact that Chapter 13 can discharge some debts that survive Chapter 7.

Related Terms

Discharge Injunction
Nondischargeable Debt
Fresh Start
Chapter 7

Browse all glossary terms →

Check your bankruptcy discharge eligibility with our free screening tool.

## What Is Dischargeable Debt in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/dischargeable-debt.html

What Is Dischargeable Debt in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Dischargeable Debt

A dischargeable debt is any debt that can be permanently eliminated through bankruptcy. Most unsecured consumer debts are dischargeable, including credit card balances, medical bills, personal loans, past-due utility bills, and many types of lawsuit judgments.

How It Works

Bankruptcy law presumes that debts are dischargeable unless they fall into one of the specific exceptions listed in 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a). This means the burden is on the creditor to prove that a debt should survive the discharge, not on the debtor to prove it should be eliminated.

Common dischargeable debts include: credit card debt, medical bills, personal loans, payday loans, past-due rent, broken leases, business debts, deficiency balances after repossession, most lawsuit judgments, and obligations under contracts the debtor rejects in bankruptcy.

Whether a specific debt is dischargeable can depend on the facts. For example, credit card charges are normally dischargeable, but charges incurred through fraud (misrepresenting income on the application) or luxury purchases over $725 within 90 days of filing may be challenged as non-dischargeable.

Key Facts

Most unsecured consumer debts are presumed dischargeable

The burden is on the creditor to prove a debt is non-dischargeable

Credit card debt, medical bills, and personal loans are almost always dischargeable

Debts from fraud or willful injury require an adversary proceeding to be declared non-dischargeable

Chapter 13 historically discharged more debts than Chapter 7 (the 'super discharge')

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Dischargeable vs Non-Dischargeable

Frequently Asked Questions

Are medical bills dischargeable?

Yes. Medical debt is one of the most commonly discharged types of debt in bankruptcy. It is general unsecured debt with no exceptions under Section 523.

Can I discharge payday loans?

Yes. Payday loans are unsecured consumer debts and are fully dischargeable. Some payday lenders attempt to claim fraud, but these challenges rarely succeed.

Are business debts dischargeable?

Yes. Business debts, including guarantees on business loans, are dischargeable. The means test does not even apply if the majority of the debtor's debts are business debts.

Related Terms

Nondischargeable Debt
Discharge
Unsecured Claim
Chapter 7

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Dismissal in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/dismissal.html

What Is Dismissal in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Dismissal

Dismissal in bankruptcy terminates the case without the debtor receiving a discharge. The automatic stay is lifted, creditors can resume collection, and the debtor's debts remain. Dismissal can be voluntary (requested by the debtor) or involuntary (ordered by the court for cause).

How It Works

A bankruptcy case can be dismissed for many reasons: the debtor fails to file required documents, misses the 341 meeting, fails to make Chapter 13 plan payments, fails the means test, or commits fraud. The debtor can also request voluntary dismissal - in Chapter 13, the debtor has an absolute right to dismiss under Section 1307(b).

Dismissal generally restores the status quo as if the bankruptcy was never filed. Liens are reinstated, any transfers avoided by the trustee may be reversed, and creditors can resume collection. However, property sold by the trustee before dismissal may not be recoverable.

There are consequences to dismissal beyond losing bankruptcy protection. If the debtor refiles within one year, the automatic stay is limited to 30 days (for one prior dismissal) or eliminated entirely (for two or more prior dismissals within the year). These limitations are found in Section 362(c)(3) and (c)(4).

Key Facts

Terminates the case without a discharge - debts remain

In Chapter 13, the debtor has an absolute right to voluntary dismissal

Common causes: failure to file documents, missed 341 meeting, failed means test

Refiling within 1 year limits the automatic stay to 30 days

Two dismissals within 1 year can eliminate the automatic stay entirely

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Dismissal Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I refile after dismissal?

Yes, but there may be consequences. If you refile within one year, the automatic stay lasts only 30 days unless you prove the new case is filed in good faith. Two dismissals within a year can eliminate the stay entirely.

Is dismissal the same as denial of discharge?

No. Dismissal ends the case without a discharge, but the debtor can refile. Denial of discharge means the debtor went through the case but was denied a discharge - typically for fraud or misconduct. The debts remain and refiling may not help.

Can I convert instead of having my case dismissed?

Often yes. In many situations, converting to a different chapter (e.g., Chapter 13 to Chapter 7) is preferable to dismissal because it preserves the automatic stay and may still result in a discharge.

Related Terms

Automatic Stay
Serial Filer
Discharge
Chapter 13

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Disposable Income in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/disposable-income.html

What Is Disposable Income in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Disposable Income

Disposable income in bankruptcy is the debtor's current monthly income minus reasonably necessary expenses as determined by the means test. In Chapter 13, all projected disposable income over the plan period must be committed to repaying unsecured creditors.

How It Works

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1325(b), if the trustee or an unsecured creditor objects to confirmation of a Chapter 13 plan, the debtor must commit all projected disposable income to the plan. For above-median debtors, expenses are calculated using IRS standards and actual secured debt payments. For below-median debtors, actual reasonable expenses are used.

The disposable income calculation is performed on Form 122C-2 for above-median debtors. Allowed deductions include taxes, mandatory payroll deductions, health insurance, child care, housing, transportation, secured debt payments, priority debt payments, and other necessary expenses.

The 'projected disposable income' concept was clarified by the Supreme Court in Hamilton v. Lanning (2010), which held that courts should use a forward-looking approach. If the debtor's income is expected to change (job loss, raise, retirement), the court can adjust the calculation to reflect anticipated future income rather than relying solely on historical figures.

Key Facts

Defined at 11 U.S.C. Section 1325(b)(2)

Above-median debtors use IRS expense standards; below-median use actual expenses

All projected disposable income must go to unsecured creditors in Chapter 13

Courts use a forward-looking approach per Hamilton v. Lanning (2010)

Calculated on Form 122C-2 (Chapter 13 full means test)

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Means Test Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep any income for myself in Chapter 13?

Yes. Disposable income is what remains after deducting all reasonably necessary expenses. You keep enough to cover housing, food, transportation, utilities, insurance, and other essential living costs. Only the surplus goes to creditors.

What if my income changes during the plan?

You can seek a plan modification. If your income increases, the trustee may also seek modification to increase payments. The court will evaluate whether the modified plan meets the disposable income test based on current circumstances.

Do I have to use IRS expense standards?

Only if you are above median income. Below-median debtors use their actual reasonable expenses. Even above-median debtors can claim actual expenses for some categories, like health care costs exceeding the IRS standard.

Related Terms

Means Test
Above Median Income
Current Monthly Income
Chapter 13

## What Is Domestic Support Obligation in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/domestic-support-obligation.html

What Is Domestic Support Obligation in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Domestic Support Obligation

A domestic support obligation (DSO) is a debt owed to a spouse, former spouse, or child for alimony, maintenance, or support established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, court order, or government unit determination. DSOs receive the highest priority in bankruptcy and cannot be discharged.

How It Works

Domestic support obligations receive special treatment throughout the Bankruptcy Code. They are non-dischargeable under Section 523(a)(5), meaning they survive both Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 bankruptcy. The debtor remains fully liable for all past-due and future support obligations.

DSOs are first priority claims under Section 507(a)(1), meaning they are paid before all other debts, including administrative expenses, tax claims, and other priority debts. In Chapter 13, the plan must provide for payment of all DSOs in full, and the debtor must remain current on post-petition DSO payments as a condition of confirmation.

The automatic stay has limited effect on DSOs. While the stay prevents collection from estate property, Section 362(b)(2) allows collection of DSOs from the debtor's post-petition income and property that is not part of the estate. State court proceedings to establish or modify support can continue despite the bankruptcy.

Key Facts

Non-dischargeable in both Chapter 7 and Chapter 13

First priority claim - paid before all other debts

The automatic stay does not prevent collection of DSOs from non-estate property

Chapter 13 plan must pay DSOs in full and debtor must stay current

Includes alimony, child support, and other support obligations

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Priority Debts

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I discharge back child support in bankruptcy?

No. Child support and all domestic support obligations are permanently non-dischargeable. Bankruptcy cannot eliminate past-due or future child support, alimony, or maintenance obligations.

Does bankruptcy stop child support enforcement?

Only partially. The automatic stay prevents collection from estate property, but enforcement agencies can continue collecting from your post-petition wages and non-estate property. Wage withholding for current support continues during bankruptcy.

What if I cannot afford my support payments?

Bankruptcy does not modify support obligations. You must seek modification through family court. In Chapter 13, the plan must pay all DSOs in full, and failure to stay current on post-petition support is grounds for dismissal.

Related Terms

Priority Claim
Nondischargeable Debt
Discharge
Chapter 13

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Estate Property in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/estate-property.html

What Is Estate Property in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Estate Property

Estate property is any property that becomes part of the bankruptcy estate when the case is filed. Under 11 U.S.C. Section 541, it includes virtually everything the debtor owns or has an interest in as of the filing date - real estate, personal property, bank accounts, investments, lawsuits, and even intangible rights.

How It Works

The scope of estate property is intentionally broad. Section 541(a)(1) includes 'all legal and equitable interests of the debtor in property as of the commencement of the case.' This catches tangible property (house, car, furniture), financial assets (bank accounts, stocks, tax refunds), and intangible interests (pending lawsuits, intellectual property, contract rights).

Certain property is excluded from the estate: most ERISA-qualified retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA), education savings accounts (529 plans), and property held in certain trusts. These exclusions operate differently from exemptions - excluded property never enters the estate at all.

Once property enters the estate, the debtor must claim exemptions to protect it from liquidation. Any non-exempt estate property can be sold by the trustee in Chapter 7. In Chapter 13, estate property is not sold, but the plan must pay unsecured creditors at least as much as the non-exempt property is worth (the best interests test).

Key Facts

Defined broadly by 11 U.S.C. Section 541 to include almost everything

Includes tangible property, financial assets, lawsuits, and intangible rights

ERISA retirement accounts are excluded (not just exempt) from the estate

In Chapter 13, post-filing earnings also become estate property

The debtor claims exemptions to protect estate property from liquidation

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Exemptions by State

Frequently Asked Questions

Does my tax refund become estate property?

Yes. Tax refunds for periods before the filing date are estate property. If you are expecting a large refund, consult with your attorney about timing. Some districts allow debtors to exempt a portion of the refund.

What about property I co-own with someone else?

Your interest in co-owned property enters the estate. In Chapter 7, the trustee can sell the property (including a co-owner's interest in some circumstances) but must protect the co-owner's share of the proceeds.

Is my engagement ring estate property?

Yes, but it is almost certainly protected by your state's personal property exemption. The distinction is that it enters the estate and you must claim the exemption to keep it.

Related Terms

Bankruptcy Estate
Exempt Property
Liquidation
Best Interests Test

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Exempt Property in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/exempt-property.html

What Is Exempt Property in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Exempt Property

Exempt property is property that the debtor is legally entitled to keep, free from creditors' claims, despite filing for bankruptcy. Exemptions are determined by state law (or federal bankruptcy exemptions in states that allow the choice) and typically protect a home, vehicle, retirement accounts, and personal belongings.

How It Works

When a debtor files bankruptcy, all property enters the bankruptcy estate. The debtor then claims exemptions on Schedule C to remove specific property from the trustee's reach. Each state has its own exemption statutes, and some states allow debtors to choose between state and federal bankruptcy exemptions.

Common exemptions include the homestead exemption (protecting equity in the debtor's primary residence), motor vehicle exemption, personal property exemptions (clothing, furniture, appliances), tools of the trade, and the wildcard exemption (protecting any property up to a dollar limit). Retirement accounts (401(k), IRA, pension) are protected by federal law regardless of state exemptions.

If the debtor claims an exemption and no party objects within 30 days, the exemption is allowed automatically. The trustee or a creditor can object to an exemption if the debtor is overclaiming - for example, claiming a homestead exemption on a rental property or valuing property too low.

Key Facts

Determined by state law - exemption amounts vary dramatically by state

Some states allow choosing between state and federal exemptions

Retirement accounts are protected by federal law (ERISA) in all states

Exemptions must be claimed on Schedule C within 14 days of the 341 meeting

Objections to exemptions must be filed within 30 days of the 341 meeting

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Exemptions by State

Frequently Asked Questions

Which states have the best exemptions?

Texas and Florida have unlimited homestead exemptions, making them the most debtor-friendly states. Kansas, Iowa, and South Dakota also have unlimited homesteads. States with low exemptions include Maryland, New Jersey, and Virginia.

Can I use federal exemptions?

Only if your state allows it. About 20 states let debtors choose between state and federal exemptions. The remaining states require debtors to use state exemptions exclusively.

What if my property is worth more than the exemption?

The trustee can sell the property, pay you the exempt amount, and distribute the remaining proceeds to creditors. This is why accurate property valuations on your schedules matter.

Related Terms

Homestead Exemption
Wildcard Exemption
Bankruptcy Estate
Estate Property

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Feasibility in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/feasibility.html

What Is Feasibility in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Feasibility

Feasibility in bankruptcy means the debtor's proposed repayment plan is realistic and the debtor can actually make all required payments. The court will not confirm a plan that the debtor is unlikely to complete. Feasibility is a mandatory requirement for plan confirmation in both Chapter 13 and Chapter 11.

How It Works

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1325(a)(6), the court must find that 'the debtor will be able to make all payments under the plan and to comply with the plan.' This is more than a mathematical exercise - the court considers the debtor's income stability, employment history, necessary expenses, and track record of making payments during the case.

The trustee frequently challenges feasibility when a debtor's budget is unrealistically tight - for example, a plan requiring the debtor to live on $200/month for food or assuming zero transportation costs. The court may also question feasibility if the debtor has a history of plan failures in prior cases.

In Chapter 11, feasibility under Section 1129(a)(11) requires that confirmation is 'not likely to be followed by the liquidation, or the need for further financial reorganization, of the debtor.' This is sometimes called the 'visionary plan' test - the plan must be grounded in reality, not wishful thinking.

Key Facts

Required for confirmation under Section 1325(a)(6) (Ch.13) and Section 1129(a)(11) (Ch.11)

The court evaluates whether the debtor can actually make all plan payments

Unrealistic budgets, unstable income, and prior failures undermine feasibility

The debtor bears the burden of proving feasibility

Post-confirmation payment history can trigger modification or dismissal

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if my plan is not feasible?

The court will deny confirmation and give you an opportunity to propose a modified plan. If no feasible plan can be proposed, the case may be dismissed or converted to Chapter 7.

How does the court evaluate feasibility?

The court looks at your income, expenses, employment stability, and whether you have been making adequate protection payments during the case. If the numbers do not add up or your budget is unrealistically lean, the court will find the plan not feasible.

Can I modify a confirmed plan if I cannot make payments?

Yes. Plan modification under Section 1329 allows you to adjust payments if your circumstances change - job loss, medical emergency, or divorce. The modified plan must still be feasible.

Related Terms

Confirmation
Chapter 13
Good Faith
Disposable Income

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Filing Fee in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/filing-fee.html

What Is Filing Fee in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Filing Fee

The filing fee is the amount charged by the bankruptcy court to file a bankruptcy petition. As of 2024, the fees are $338 for Chapter 7, $313 for Chapter 13, and $1,738 for Chapter 11. Debtors who cannot afford the fee may request installment payments or, in Chapter 7, a fee waiver.

How It Works

Bankruptcy filing fees are set by the Judicial Conference of the United States and are the same in every federal district. The fee must be paid when the petition is filed, unless the debtor files an application to pay in installments or a fee waiver request.

Installment payments are available in all chapters. The debtor files an application (Official Form 103A) proposing to pay the fee in up to four installments within 120 days of filing (extendable to 180 days for cause). The court usually approves these applications routinely.

A complete fee waiver (Official Form 103B) is available only in Chapter 7 and only if the debtor's income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. There is no fee waiver in Chapter 13, Chapter 11, or Chapter 12. If installments are approved but the debtor fails to pay, the case can be dismissed.

Key Facts

Chapter 7: $338 | Chapter 13: $313 | Chapter 11: $1,738 | Chapter 12: $278

Installment payments available in all chapters (up to 4 payments in 120 days)

Fee waivers only available in Chapter 7 for income below 150% of poverty guidelines

Fees are the same in every federal district

Failure to pay installments can result in case dismissal

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Bankruptcy Cost Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get the filing fee waived?

Only in Chapter 7, and only if your household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. You must file Official Form 103B. There is no fee waiver available in Chapter 13 or Chapter 11.

Is the filing fee the only cost of filing bankruptcy?

No. The filing fee is the court cost only. Attorney fees, credit counseling courses, and financial management courses are additional costs. Total out-of-pocket costs for a Chapter 7 with an attorney typically range from $1,500-$3,500.

Do I have to pay the filing fee before my case starts?

Not necessarily. You can request installment payments and have the first payment due 30 days after filing. However, the petition is not fully filed until the fee is paid or an installment application is approved.

Related Terms

Bankruptcy Petition
Chapter 7
Chapter 13
Petition Preparer

## What Is Fresh Start in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/fresh-start.html

What Is Fresh Start in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Fresh Start

The fresh start is the fundamental purpose of bankruptcy law - giving honest but unfortunate debtors a new beginning free from the burden of overwhelming debt. The Supreme Court has described the fresh start as 'a new opportunity in life, unhampered by the pressure and discouragement of pre-existing debt.'

How It Works

The fresh start doctrine is not a single statute but a guiding principle woven throughout bankruptcy law. The discharge eliminates legal liability for pre-bankruptcy debts. The discharge injunction prevents creditors from collecting discharged debts. Exemptions allow the debtor to keep essential property. Together, these protections give the debtor a clean financial slate.

The fresh start is available only to 'honest but unfortunate debtors.' Debtors who commit fraud, conceal assets, or abuse the bankruptcy system may be denied a discharge under Section 727(a). The means test under Section 707(b) prevents abuse of Chapter 7 by debtors who can afford to repay their debts.

Research shows that the fresh start works. Studies of debtors who receive a discharge show significant improvements in credit scores, home ownership rates, and overall financial stability within 2-3 years. The ability to file bankruptcy also encourages entrepreneurship by reducing the personal risk of business failure.

Key Facts

The Supreme Court has described the fresh start as bankruptcy's 'central purpose'

Available only to 'honest but unfortunate' debtors - fraud disqualifies

Implemented through the discharge, discharge injunction, and exemptions

Credit scores typically begin recovering within 12-18 months of discharge

The fresh start enables entrepreneurship by limiting personal risk

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Rebuild Credit Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to rebuild after bankruptcy?

Most people see meaningful credit improvement within 12-18 months. FHA mortgages are available 2 years after Chapter 7 discharge. New credit cards (secured) are often available within weeks of discharge.

Can I file bankruptcy more than once?

Yes, but there are time limits. You must wait 8 years between Chapter 7 discharges, 6 years between a Chapter 7 and Chapter 13, and 2 years between Chapter 13 discharges. These are measured from filing date to filing date.

Will employers know I filed bankruptcy?

Bankruptcy filings are public records, but most employers do not check bankruptcy records. Federal law prohibits government employers from discriminating based on bankruptcy. Private employer protections vary by state and circuit.

Related Terms

Discharge
Discharge Injunction
Exempt Property
Chapter 7

Browse all glossary terms →

Check your bankruptcy discharge eligibility with our free screening tool.

## What Is Good Faith in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/good-faith.html

What Is Good Faith in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Good Faith

Good faith in bankruptcy means the debtor filed the case and proposed the repayment plan for legitimate purposes rather than to abuse the bankruptcy system. Courts evaluate good faith based on the totality of the circumstances, including the debtor's honesty, the accuracy of the schedules, and the sincerity of the repayment effort.

How It Works

Good faith is required at two stages in Chapter 13: the petition must be filed in good faith under Section 1325(a)(7), and the plan must be proposed in good faith under Section 1325(a)(3). Courts apply a multi-factor test that varies by circuit but generally considers: the accuracy of the schedules, the debtor's motivation for filing, the degree of effort in the plan, whether the plan pays a meaningful amount to unsecured creditors, and any prior bankruptcy history.

A debtor who files solely to delay a single creditor, proposes a plan paying nothing to unsecured creditors when they could afford to pay more, or files immediately after a lavish spending spree may be found to have filed in bad faith. Similarly, a debtor who serially files and dismisses cases to keep the automatic stay in place may be denied good faith.

Good faith also applies in Chapter 11 under Section 1129(a)(3). The plan must be proposed in good faith and not by any means forbidden by law. Chapter 7 does not have an explicit good faith requirement for filing, but the means test and Section 707(b)(3) serve a similar gatekeeping function.

Key Facts

Required for both the petition (Section 1325(a)(7)) and the plan (Section 1325(a)(3))

Evaluated under a totality of the circumstances test

Filing to delay a single creditor or after lavish spending can indicate bad faith

Serial filers face heightened good faith scrutiny

The good faith determination is within the bankruptcy judge's broad discretion

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Good Faith in Chapter 13

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a bad faith filing?

A bad faith filing is one made for an improper purpose - to delay a specific creditor, to shelter assets through repeated filings, or without any sincere intent to reorganize. Common indicators include serial filings, manipulated income, and plans that pay nothing to unsecured creditors.

Can my case be dismissed for bad faith?

Yes. Under Section 1307(c), the court can dismiss a Chapter 13 case for cause, including lack of good faith. In Chapter 7, Section 707(b)(3) allows dismissal if the filing is an abuse of Chapter 7 based on the totality of circumstances.

Does paying unsecured creditors 0% mean bad faith?

Not automatically. If the debtor has no disposable income after paying secured debts, priority debts, and necessary expenses, a 0% plan can still be proposed in good faith. The court looks at the overall circumstances, not just the percentage.

Related Terms

Confirmation
Feasibility
Disposable Income
Dismissal

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Homestead Exemption in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/homestead-exemption.html

What Is Homestead Exemption in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Homestead Exemption

The homestead exemption protects equity in the debtor's primary residence from being seized to pay creditors in bankruptcy. The amount of protection varies dramatically by state - from as little as $5,000 in some states to unlimited in Texas, Florida, Kansas, Iowa, and South Dakota.

How It Works

The homestead exemption protects a specified dollar amount of equity in the debtor's primary residence. If the debtor's home equity is at or below the exemption limit, the trustee cannot sell the home. If equity exceeds the exemption, the trustee may sell the home but must pay the debtor the exempt amount from the sale proceeds.

State exemption amounts vary enormously. Texas and Florida offer unlimited homestead exemptions - a debtor could have $10 million in home equity and it would be fully protected. At the other extreme, states like New Jersey and Maryland offer exemptions of only $25,000 or less. Some states allow married couples to double the exemption.

BAPCPA imposed a cap on homestead exemptions for recently purchased homes: if the debtor acquired the home within 1,215 days (about 3.3 years) of filing, the exemption is capped at $189,050 (adjusted periodically) regardless of state law. This prevents debtors from buying expensive homes in unlimited-exemption states right before filing.

Key Facts

Protects equity in the debtor's primary residence

Amounts vary by state: from $5,000 (some states) to unlimited (TX, FL, KS, IA, SD)

BAPCPA caps exemption at $189,050 for homes purchased within 1,215 days of filing

Only applies to the debtor's principal residence, not investment properties

Some states allow married couples to double (or 'stack') the exemption

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Exemptions by State

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my house in bankruptcy?

In most cases, yes. If your home equity is within your state's homestead exemption and you are current on mortgage payments, you keep your home. Even in states with low exemptions, many homeowners have little equity and are protected.

What counts as equity for the homestead exemption?

Equity is the fair market value of the home minus all mortgages, liens, and costs of sale. If your home is worth $250,000 and you owe $230,000, your equity is approximately $20,000 (minus hypothetical sale costs).

Can I exempt a mobile home?

In most states, yes, if it is your primary residence. Some states have separate mobile home exemptions. The homestead exemption generally applies to any dwelling the debtor uses as their primary residence.

Related Terms

Exempt Property
Estate Property
Wildcard Exemption
Chapter 7

## What Is Involuntary Petition in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/involuntary-petition.html

What Is Involuntary Petition in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Involuntary Petition

An involuntary petition is a bankruptcy case filed against a debtor by creditors without the debtor's consent. It requires at least three creditors holding undisputed, unsecured claims totaling at least $18,600 and is available only under Chapter 7 or Chapter 11. Involuntary filings are rare and carry significant risks for creditors.

How It Works

Involuntary petitions are governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 303. If the debtor has 12 or more creditors, three must join the petition. If fewer than 12, a single creditor may file. The petitioning creditors must hold non-contingent, undisputed, unsecured claims totaling at least $18,600 (adjusted periodically).

The debtor can contest the involuntary petition. The court will enter an order for relief (allowing the bankruptcy to proceed) only if the debtor is generally not paying debts as they become due, or a custodee, receiver, or general agent was appointed within 120 days before the petition. The debtor has 21 days to respond.

Creditors face significant risk if the involuntary petition is dismissed. Under Section 303(i), the court can award the debtor costs, attorney fees, actual damages, and - if the petition was filed in bad faith - punitive damages and compensatory damages for loss of business.

Key Facts

Requires 3+ creditors with $18,600+ in undisputed, unsecured claims

Available only under Chapter 7 and Chapter 11 - not Chapter 13 or 12

The debtor can contest and has 21 days to respond

Cannot be filed against farmers, family farmers, or nonprofits

Bad faith filing exposes creditors to punitive damages

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Involuntary Petitions

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a single creditor file an involuntary petition?

Only if the debtor has fewer than 12 creditors total. If the debtor has 12 or more creditors, at least three must join the petition.

How common are involuntary petitions?

Very rare. Fewer than 1% of bankruptcy cases are involuntary. They are most commonly used against businesses that are dissipating assets while ignoring creditors.

What happens if the involuntary petition is dismissed?

The filing creditors may be ordered to pay the debtor's attorney fees, costs, and actual damages. If the petition was filed in bad faith, punitive damages are also available. This risk deters frivolous involuntary filings.

Related Terms

Bankruptcy Petition
Voluntary Petition
Chapter 7
Chapter 11

## What Is Lien Avoidance in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/lien-avoidance.html

What Is Lien Avoidance in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Lien Avoidance

Lien avoidance is the process of removing certain liens from the debtor's property in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(f). It applies primarily to judicial liens and non-possessory, non-purchase-money security interests that impair the debtor's exemptions.

How It Works

Under Section 522(f), a debtor can avoid (remove) a judicial lien if it impairs an exemption the debtor would otherwise be entitled to claim. The formula compares the total liens plus the exemption to the property's value. If the liens plus exemption exceed the value, the judicial lien impairs the exemption and can be avoided.

The process requires filing a motion to avoid the lien, serving the lienholder, and obtaining a court order. The debtor must demonstrate that the lien is a judicial lien (not a consensual lien like a mortgage), that the property is exempt (or would be exempt but for the lien), and that the lien impairs the exemption.

Lien avoidance also applies to non-possessory, non-purchase-money security interests in certain categories of property: household goods, tools of the trade, and health aids. This prevents creditors from taking blanket security interests in household items to circumvent exemptions.

Key Facts

Governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 522(f)

Applies to judicial liens that impair exemptions

Does NOT apply to consensual liens (mortgages, car loans)

Also avoids security interests in household goods and tools of the trade

Requires filing a motion and obtaining a court order

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Lien Avoidance

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I avoid a mortgage lien?

No. Section 522(f) only applies to judicial liens and certain non-purchase-money security interests. Consensual liens like mortgages and car loans cannot be avoided through this mechanism.

What is the difference between lien avoidance and lien stripping?

Lien avoidance (Section 522(f)) removes judicial liens that impair exemptions. Lien stripping (typically in Chapter 13) removes wholly unsecured junior liens from property. They are different tools under different code sections.

Do I have to go to court to avoid a lien?

Yes. Lien avoidance requires filing a motion, serving the lienholder with notice, and obtaining a court order. The lienholder can oppose the motion if they believe the exemption is not impaired.

Related Terms

Lien
Lien Stripping
Exempt Property
Homestead Exemption

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Lien Stripping in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/lien-stripping.html

What Is Lien Stripping in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Lien Stripping

Lien stripping is the process of removing a junior mortgage or lien from the debtor's property in Chapter 13 bankruptcy when the property is worth less than the balance of the senior lien. The junior lien is reclassified as unsecured debt, allowing it to be discharged at the end of the plan.

How It Works

Lien stripping is available in Chapter 13 (and Chapter 11 for individuals) when a junior lien is wholly unsecured. For example, if a home is worth $200,000 and the first mortgage balance is $220,000, a second mortgage of $50,000 is wholly unsecured - there is no equity to secure it. The second mortgage can be stripped and treated as unsecured debt.

The debtor files a motion to value the collateral (sometimes called a motion to strip lien) under Section 506(a). If the court finds the junior lien is wholly unsecured, it reclassifies the claim as unsecured. The stripped lien is treated like credit card debt in the plan and may receive only pennies on the dollar.

After completing all Chapter 13 plan payments and receiving a discharge, the stripped lien is permanently removed. The debtor should record the court order with the county recorder's office to clear the title. Lien stripping is not available in Chapter 7 under the Supreme Court's decision in Dewsnup v. Timm (1992).

Key Facts

Available in Chapter 13 and individual Chapter 11 - NOT Chapter 7

Requires the junior lien to be wholly unsecured (no equity behind the senior lien)

The stripped lien is treated as unsecured debt in the plan

Permanent removal occurs upon Chapter 13 discharge

Based on Section 506(a) valuation of the secured claim

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Lien Stripping Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I strip a second mortgage in Chapter 7?

No. The Supreme Court held in Dewsnup v. Timm (1992) that lien stripping is not available in Chapter 7. You must file Chapter 13 (or individual Chapter 11) to strip a junior lien.

What if the junior lien is partially secured?

If there is even $1 of equity behind the senior lien, the junior lien is partially secured and cannot be stripped. Lien stripping only applies to wholly unsecured junior liens.

How do I prove my home is underwater?

You will need a current appraisal or broker's price opinion showing the home's fair market value. The court compares this value to the outstanding balance of the senior lien.

Related Terms

Lien
Lien Avoidance
Secured Claim
Chapter 13

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Lien in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/lien.html

What Is Lien in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Lien

A lien is a legal right or interest that a creditor has in the debtor's property as security for a debt. Common liens include mortgage liens on real estate, security interests in vehicles, judgment liens from lawsuits, and tax liens. Liens generally survive bankruptcy even when the underlying debt is discharged.

How It Works

Liens give creditors a secured interest in specific property. If the debtor does not pay, the lienholder can foreclose on real estate or repossess personal property to satisfy the debt. In bankruptcy, liens are treated differently from unsecured debts - they attach to the property, not just the debtor personally.

When a debtor receives a discharge, the personal obligation to pay the debt is eliminated, but the lien remains on the property. This means a mortgage lender can still foreclose if payments are not made, even after discharge. To fully clear a lien, the debtor must either pay it, avoid it (if avoidable under Section 522(f)), strip it (if the property is underwater), or surrender the property.

There are three main types of liens: consensual liens (mortgages, car loans), judicial liens (from court judgments), and statutory liens (tax liens, mechanic's liens). Different types of liens have different vulnerability to avoidance in bankruptcy. Judicial liens on exempt property can be avoided under Section 522(f), while consensual and statutory liens generally cannot.

Key Facts

Liens survive bankruptcy discharge - they attach to property, not the person

Three types: consensual (mortgage), judicial (judgment), and statutory (tax)

Judicial liens on exempt property can be avoided under Section 522(f)

The discharge eliminates personal liability but does not remove the lien

Liens are valued as secured claims up to the value of the collateral

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Liens in Bankruptcy

Frequently Asked Questions

Does bankruptcy remove liens?

Generally no. Bankruptcy discharges personal liability but leaves liens intact. However, certain liens can be avoided (judicial liens on exempt property under Section 522(f)) or stripped (junior liens on underwater homes in Chapter 13).

What is a judgment lien?

A judgment lien is created when a creditor wins a lawsuit and records the judgment against the debtor's property (usually real estate). Unlike a mortgage, the debtor did not consent to this lien. Judgment liens on exempt property can often be avoided in bankruptcy.

What happens to my car lien in bankruptcy?

In Chapter 7, you must continue paying or surrender the vehicle. In Chapter 13, you can pay through the plan, and if the loan is more than 910 days old, you may be able to cram down the secured claim to the vehicle's current value.

Related Terms

Lien Avoidance
Lien Stripping
Secured Claim
Automatic Stay

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Liquidation in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/liquidation.html

What Is Liquidation in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Liquidation

Liquidation in bankruptcy refers to the sale of the debtor's non-exempt property by the trustee to pay creditors. Chapter 7 is known as a liquidation bankruptcy because the trustee's primary role is to convert assets into cash for distribution. In practice, most Chapter 7 cases are 'no-asset' cases where nothing is liquidated.

How It Works

In Chapter 7, the trustee reviews the debtor's schedules and investigates whether any non-exempt assets exist. If the trustee identifies property worth selling, they file a notice of intent to sell and conduct the sale. The proceeds are distributed to creditors in the order of priority established by the Bankruptcy Code.

Distribution follows a strict hierarchy: secured creditors are paid from their collateral, then administrative expenses (trustee fees, attorney fees), then domestic support obligations, then other priority claims (taxes, wages), and finally general unsecured creditors. If funds are insufficient to pay all claims in a class, distribution is pro rata within that class.

Approximately 95% of Chapter 7 cases are no-asset cases, meaning the trustee finds no property worth liquidating after exemptions. In these cases, the trustee files a report of no distribution and the case proceeds to discharge without any property being sold.

Key Facts

Chapter 7 is called 'liquidation' bankruptcy

About 95% of Chapter 7 cases are no-asset - nothing is sold

Distribution order: secured -> administrative -> priority -> general unsecured

The trustee handles all sales and distributions

Exempt property is not subject to liquidation

Frequently Asked Questions

Will the trustee sell my belongings?

In most cases, no. Personal belongings (clothing, furniture, appliances) are almost always fully exempt. The trustee targets high-value non-exempt assets: non-exempt home equity, valuable vehicles, investment accounts, and tax refunds.

What is a no-asset case?

A no-asset case is a Chapter 7 case where the trustee determines there are no non-exempt assets worth selling. Approximately 95% of consumer Chapter 7 cases are no-asset. Creditors do not need to file proofs of claim in no-asset cases.

Can I buy back property from the trustee?

Sometimes. If the trustee is selling property, you may be able to purchase it back at the sale. Some trustees will negotiate a buyback if you can pay the non-exempt equity amount. This can be useful for sentimental items or property with value to you beyond its market price.

Related Terms

Chapter 7
Case Trustee
Exempt Property
No-Asset Case

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Means Test in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/means-test.html

What Is Means Test in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Means Test

The means test is a formula that determines whether a debtor qualifies for Chapter 7 bankruptcy based on their income and expenses. Introduced by BAPCPA in 2005, it compares the debtor's income to the state median and calculates disposable income to prevent higher-income debtors from abusing Chapter 7.

How It Works

The means test has two stages. First, the debtor's annualized current monthly income is compared to the median income for their state and household size. If below the median, the debtor passes automatically and can file Chapter 7 without further calculation.

If above the median, the debtor must complete the full means test on Form 122A-2. This calculation deducts standardized expenses (using IRS Local and National Standards), actual secured debt payments, priority debt payments, and certain other allowed expenses from CMI. If the resulting disposable income is too high, the case is presumed abusive and may be dismissed or converted to Chapter 13.

The means test does not apply if the debtor's debts are primarily business debts (more than 50% of total debt is non-consumer). It also does not apply to disabled veterans whose debts were incurred primarily during active duty. Even if a debtor fails the means test, the presumption of abuse can be rebutted by showing special circumstances.

Key Facts

Introduced by BAPCPA in 2005 to prevent Chapter 7 abuse

Step 1: Compare income to state median for household size

Step 2 (above median only): Calculate disposable income using IRS standards

Does not apply to primarily business debt or disabled veterans

Presumption of abuse can be rebutted by 'special circumstances'

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Means Test Calculator

Frequently Asked Questions

What if I fail the means test?

You can file Chapter 13 instead, attempt to rebut the presumption of abuse with special circumstances (such as a medical condition or recently reduced income), or wait until your 6-month income average drops below the threshold.

Does the means test look at household expenses?

For above-median debtors, expenses are calculated using IRS standards (national and local), not actual expenses. You get the IRS-allowed amount for housing, food, transportation, and healthcare, plus actual payments on secured debts and priority claims.

Can I avoid the means test?

If your debts are primarily business debts (more than 50%), the means test does not apply. Otherwise, all Chapter 7 filers must complete at least the first part of the means test (income comparison).

Related Terms

Above Median Income
Current Monthly Income
Disposable Income
Chapter 7

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Meeting of Creditors in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/meeting-of-creditors.html

What Is Meeting of Creditors in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Meeting of Creditors

The meeting of creditors, also called the 341 meeting, is a mandatory hearing in every bankruptcy case where the debtor is questioned under oath by the trustee and any creditors who attend. Despite its name, creditors rarely appear in consumer cases. The meeting typically lasts 5 to 15 minutes.

How It Works

The meeting of creditors is required by 11 U.S.C. Section 341(a) and is scheduled approximately 21-40 days after the petition is filed. The debtor must attend, present government-issued photo identification and proof of Social Security number, and answer questions about the accuracy and completeness of the bankruptcy schedules.

The trustee conducts the meeting and asks standard questions: Did you list all your assets? Did you list all your debts? Have you made any transfers of property in the last few years? Is all the information in your petition true and correct? The trustee may also ask follow-up questions about specific assets, income, or transactions.

Creditors have the right to attend and ask questions, but in consumer cases they almost never do. The meeting is not held in a courtroom and the judge does not attend. After the meeting, creditors have 60 days to file complaints objecting to the debtor's discharge or the dischargeability of specific debts.

Key Facts

Required by 11 U.S.C. Section 341(a) in every bankruptcy case

Scheduled 21-40 days after filing

The debtor testifies under oath

No judge is present - the trustee runs the meeting

Creditors rarely attend in consumer cases

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: 341 Meeting Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a lawyer at the 341 meeting?

If you have an attorney, they will attend with you. If you are pro se, you attend alone. Having an attorney is helpful because they can prepare you for questions, but many pro se debtors successfully navigate the meeting.

What documents do I need to bring?

You must bring a government-issued photo ID (driver's license, passport) and proof of your Social Security number (Social Security card, tax return, W-2). Some trustees require recent pay stubs and bank statements as well.

Can the 341 meeting be done by phone?

Many districts now allow telephonic or video 341 meetings, especially since COVID-19. Check with your local court or trustee for the current policy. Some districts have returned to in-person meetings while others remain virtual.

Related Terms

341 Meeting
Case Trustee
Discharge
Bankruptcy Petition

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Motion for Relief from Stay in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/motion-for-relief-from-stay.html

What Is Motion for Relief from Stay in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Motion for Relief from Stay

A motion for relief from stay is a request by a creditor asking the bankruptcy court to lift the automatic stay so the creditor can take action against the debtor or the debtor's property - typically to foreclose on a home or repossess a vehicle. The court grants relief if the creditor lacks adequate protection or the debtor has no equity in the property.

How It Works

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(d), a secured creditor can seek relief from the automatic stay on two grounds: (1) lack of adequate protection of the creditor's interest in the property (the collateral is losing value without compensation), or (2) the debtor has no equity in the property and the property is not necessary for an effective reorganization.

The creditor files a motion and the court schedules a hearing, typically within 30 days. The debtor and trustee can oppose the motion by demonstrating adequate protection (making current payments, property is not declining in value) or by showing the property is essential to the reorganization (e.g., the debtor's home in Chapter 13).

If the court grants relief, the creditor can proceed with foreclosure or repossession outside of the bankruptcy case. The court may grant full relief (completely lifting the stay) or limited relief (allowing the creditor to proceed to a certain point, such as completing a foreclosure sale but not evicting the debtor).

Key Facts

Governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 362(d)

Two grounds: lack of adequate protection OR no equity and property not needed for reorganization

Hearing must be held within 30 days of the motion

The debtor/trustee bear the burden on the equity issue; the movant on all other issues

The court can grant full or limited relief from the stay

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Relief from Stay

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I oppose a motion for relief from stay?

File a written response before the hearing deadline, attend the hearing, and present evidence of adequate protection - proof you are making current payments, the property is not declining in value, and (in Chapter 13) you need the property for your reorganization.

How quickly can a creditor get relief from stay?

The hearing is typically set within 30 days. If the debtor does not respond or the motion is unopposed, relief can be granted quickly. In emergencies (waste, destruction of collateral), creditors can seek expedited relief.

What is 'comfort order' relief?

Sometimes creditors seek 'comfort order' relief - a court order confirming that the stay does not apply to their specific situation. This is common when the creditor is unsure whether the stay covers their intended action.

Related Terms

Automatic Stay
Adequate Protection
Stay Violation
Secured Claim

Browse all glossary terms →

Check your bankruptcy discharge eligibility with our free screening tool.

## What Is No-Asset Case in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/no-asset-case.html

What Is No-Asset Case in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › No-Asset Case

A no-asset case is a Chapter 7 bankruptcy case in which the trustee determines there is no non-exempt property available to liquidate and distribute to creditors. Approximately 95% of consumer Chapter 7 cases are no-asset cases, meaning creditors receive nothing from the estate.

How It Works

After reviewing the debtor's schedules and conducting the 341 meeting, the Chapter 7 trustee evaluates whether any non-exempt assets exist. If all property is either exempt, subject to valid liens exceeding the property's value, or worth too little to justify the cost of sale, the trustee files a report of no distribution.

In a no-asset case, creditors are not required to file proofs of claim because there will be no distribution. The court sends a notice informing creditors that it appears to be a no-asset case. If the trustee later discovers assets, the case can be converted to an asset case and creditors will be given an opportunity to file claims.

No-asset cases proceed more quickly and simply than asset cases. There is no need for the trustee to sell property, resolve disputes over asset values, or make distributions. The case typically moves from the 341 meeting to discharge in about 60 days.

Key Facts

Approximately 95% of consumer Chapter 7 cases are no-asset

The trustee files a 'report of no distribution'

Creditors do not need to file proofs of claim in no-asset cases

The case can be converted to asset if the trustee later discovers property

No-asset cases typically result in faster discharge

Frequently Asked Questions

If it is a no-asset case, why did I need to list everything?

Federal law requires full disclosure of all assets regardless of whether they are exempt. Failure to list assets is bankruptcy fraud and can result in denial of discharge, case dismissal, or criminal prosecution.

Can a no-asset case become an asset case?

Yes. If the trustee discovers previously undisclosed property, a pending lawsuit with value, or a preference payment worth recovering, the case can be reopened as an asset case. Creditors will then be given notice and an opportunity to file claims.

Does no-asset mean creditors get nothing?

From the bankruptcy estate, yes - creditors receive no distribution. However, creditors with non-dischargeable debts (student loans, certain taxes, support obligations) can still collect after the case closes.

Related Terms

Chapter 7
Case Trustee
Liquidation
Exempt Property

Browse all glossary terms →
