## What Is Nondischargeable Debt in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/nondischargeable-debt.html

What Is Nondischargeable Debt in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Nondischargeable Debt

A nondischargeable debt is a debt that survives bankruptcy and must still be paid after the case concludes. Common nondischargeable debts include student loans, recent tax obligations, child support and alimony, debts from fraud, DUI-related judgments, and criminal fines.

How It Works

The categories of nondischargeable debt are listed in 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a). Some debts are automatically nondischargeable (taxes, student loans, support obligations), while others require the creditor to file an adversary proceeding within 60 days of the 341 meeting to have the debt declared nondischargeable (fraud, willful injury, embezzlement).

The most commonly encountered nondischargeable debts are: (1) domestic support obligations (child support, alimony); (2) most student loans (unless the debtor proves 'undue hardship'); (3) income taxes less than 3 years old, or where no return was filed, or based on a fraudulent return; (4) debts obtained through fraud or false pretenses; and (5) debts from willful and malicious injury.

The determination of nondischargeability can be different between Chapter 7 and Chapter 13. Historically, Chapter 13 offered a broader discharge (the 'super discharge') that could discharge some debts surviving Chapter 7, but BAPCPA narrowed this advantage significantly.

Key Facts

Listed in 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a) - 19 categories

Some are automatic (taxes, support); others require creditor action (fraud)

Student loans are nondischargeable unless 'undue hardship' is proven

Creditors must file an adversary proceeding within 60 days of the 341 meeting for fraud-based claims

The debtor remains personally liable for nondischargeable debts after bankruptcy

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Non-Dischargeable Debts

Frequently Asked Questions

Are student loans ever dischargeable?

Rarely. The debtor must prove 'undue hardship' through an adversary proceeding. Most courts apply the Brunner test, which requires showing: (1) the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living while repaying, (2) this situation is likely to persist, and (3) the debtor made good faith efforts to repay.

What taxes survive bankruptcy?

Income taxes are nondischargeable if: the return was due less than 3 years before filing, the return was filed less than 2 years before filing, or the tax was assessed less than 240 days before filing. Taxes from fraudulent returns or unfiled returns are always nondischargeable.

Can I discharge debts from a car accident?

Debts from a regular car accident (negligence) are dischargeable. However, debts from a DUI/DWI-related accident are nondischargeable under Section 523(a)(9). The distinction is whether alcohol or drugs were involved.

Related Terms

Dischargeable Debt
Discharge
Adversary Proceeding
Priority Claim

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Objection to Discharge in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/objection-to-discharge.html

What Is Objection to Discharge in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Objection to Discharge

An objection to discharge is a legal action seeking to deny the debtor's overall discharge in bankruptcy, preventing the elimination of any debts. This is different from a nondischargeability complaint, which targets only specific debts. Objections to discharge are based on debtor misconduct such as fraud, concealment, or destruction of records.

How It Works

Objections to discharge are governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a) and must be filed as adversary proceedings within 60 days after the first date set for the 341 meeting. The U.S. Trustee, the case trustee, or any creditor can file an objection.

The grounds for denying discharge include: the debtor is not an individual (corporations do not receive a discharge); the debtor transferred, destroyed, or concealed property with intent to defraud within one year of filing; the debtor destroyed or concealed financial records; the debtor made a false oath or account; the debtor failed to explain a loss of assets; or the debtor refused to obey a lawful court order.

If the court denies the debtor's discharge, none of the debtor's debts are eliminated. This is the most severe sanction in bankruptcy - the debtor goes through the entire process without receiving any relief. Denial of discharge also prevents the debtor from receiving a discharge in a subsequent case for the same debts.

Key Facts

Governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a) - denies ALL discharge, not just one debt

Must be filed within 60 days of the first 341 meeting date

Grounds include fraud, concealment, false oath, and destruction of records

Can be filed by the trustee, U.S. Trustee, or any creditor

Only applies in Chapter 7 - Chapter 13 does not have a Section 727 equivalent

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Section 727 Objections

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between denial of discharge and nondischargeability?

Denial of discharge (Section 727) prevents the debtor from discharging ANY debts - it is a total bar. Nondischargeability (Section 523) makes only specific debts survive the discharge. Denial of discharge is for debtor misconduct; nondischargeability is about the nature of the debt.

Can my discharge be denied for honest mistakes?

Generally no. Section 727 requires intentional misconduct - concealment, fraud, false statements. Honest errors in the schedules, while they should be corrected by amendment, typically do not rise to the level of grounds for denial of discharge.

Who usually files objections to discharge?

The case trustee or the U.S. Trustee most commonly file Section 727 complaints. Individual creditors occasionally file them, but it is less common because the expense of litigation benefits all creditors, not just the one filing.

Related Terms

Discharge
Nondischargeable Debt
Adversary Proceeding
341 Meeting

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Petition Preparer in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/petition-preparer.html

What Is Petition Preparer in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Petition Preparer

A petition preparer is a non-attorney who assists debtors in preparing bankruptcy forms and documents for filing. Petition preparers can type forms and organize paperwork but cannot provide legal advice, explain legal options, or represent the debtor in court. They are regulated by 11 U.S.C. Section 110.

How It Works

Petition preparers fill a gap between full attorney representation and completely self-represented filing. They help pro se debtors complete the official bankruptcy forms - the petition, schedules, means test, and statement of financial affairs - by typing the debtor's information into the correct forms.

Section 110 strictly prohibits petition preparers from offering legal advice. They cannot tell the debtor which chapter to file, how to value property, which exemptions to claim, or how to handle specific legal issues. They can only provide typing services. Petition preparers must sign all documents they prepare, include their name and Social Security number, and charge reasonable fees.

Violations of Section 110 can result in fines up to $500 per violation, disgorgement of fees, and injunctions. Petition preparers who provide unauthorized legal advice (practicing law without a license) face additional penalties under state law.

Key Facts

Regulated by 11 U.S.C. Section 110

Cannot provide legal advice - typing services only

Must sign all documents prepared and disclose fees charged

Fees are subject to court review and can be disgorged if unreasonable

Violations can result in fines, fee disgorgement, and injunctions

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: File Without a Lawyer

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I use a petition preparer instead of a lawyer?

A petition preparer costs less than an attorney ($100-$400 vs. $1,500-$3,500) but cannot advise you on any legal issues. If your case is straightforward, a preparer may be sufficient. If you have property to protect, debts to challenge, or complex income, an attorney is strongly recommended.

How much does a petition preparer charge?

Fees typically range from $100 to $400. The court can review the fee and order disgorgement if it is unreasonable. This is significantly less than attorney fees but comes with the limitation of no legal advice.

Can a petition preparer represent me in court?

No. Petition preparers cannot appear in court, file motions, or represent you in any legal proceeding. Only attorneys can represent debtors in bankruptcy court. If issues arise during your case, you would need to hire an attorney or handle them pro se.

Related Terms

Bankruptcy Petition
Schedules
Filing Fee
Voluntary Petition

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Plan Modification in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/plan-modification.html

What Is Plan Modification in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Plan Modification

Plan modification is a change to a confirmed Chapter 13 repayment plan, requested when the debtor's financial circumstances change during the 3 to 5-year plan period. Modifications can increase or decrease payments, extend the plan duration, or alter the treatment of specific creditors.

How It Works

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1329, the debtor, trustee, or holder of an unsecured claim can request modification of a confirmed Chapter 13 plan. Modifications are common because financial circumstances frequently change over a multi-year plan - job changes, medical emergencies, divorce, or increases in income.

A proposed modification must still meet all the requirements for initial confirmation: good faith, best interests test, feasibility, and commitment of disposable income. The court holds a hearing on the proposed modification and creditors can object. The plan can be extended but generally not beyond five years from the original first payment date.

Common modifications include: reducing payments due to job loss or income reduction, increasing payments due to income increase (often initiated by the trustee), adding newly filed claims, adjusting for changes in secured debt (paying off a car loan), and surrendering property that was originally being retained.

Key Facts

Governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 1329

Can be requested by the debtor, trustee, or unsecured creditor

Modified plan must meet all original confirmation requirements

Plan can be extended but generally not beyond 5 years from the first payment

Common trigger: job loss, medical emergency, or income change

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Plan Modification

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the trustee force me to increase my payments?

Yes. If your income increases during the plan, the trustee can file a motion to modify the plan to capture the additional disposable income. The court will evaluate whether modification is warranted based on the change in circumstances.

How many times can I modify my plan?

There is no statutory limit on the number of modifications. However, frequent modifications may raise concerns about feasibility and good faith. Each modification requires court approval.

Can I extend my plan beyond 5 years?

Generally no. Section 1329(c) limits the plan to 60 months from the date of the first payment. However, some courts have allowed extensions beyond 5 years in extraordinary circumstances - this is an unsettled area of law.

Related Terms

Chapter 13
Confirmation
Feasibility
Disposable Income

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Preference in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/preference.html

What Is Preference in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Preference

A preference is a payment or transfer made by the debtor to a creditor within 90 days before filing bankruptcy (or one year for insiders) that gives that creditor more than it would have received in a Chapter 7 liquidation. The trustee can avoid (recover) preferential transfers to distribute the funds equally among all creditors.

How It Works

Preference law, codified at 11 U.S.C. Section 547, is based on a simple principle of fairness: a debtor should not be able to pick and choose which creditors to pay in the period leading up to bankruptcy. If one creditor gets paid while others do not, the payment can be clawed back and distributed equally.

To establish a preference, the trustee must prove six elements: (1) a transfer of the debtor's property, (2) to or for the benefit of a creditor, (3) on account of an antecedent debt, (4) made while the debtor was insolvent, (5) within 90 days before filing (1 year for insiders), and (6) that gave the creditor more than it would have received in Chapter 7 liquidation.

Several defenses exist: the contemporaneous exchange defense (the creditor gave new value at the time of the transfer), the ordinary course of business defense (the payment was consistent with prior dealing), the subsequent new value defense (the creditor extended additional credit after the payment), and the small transfer defense ($7,575 or less for non-business debts).

Key Facts

Governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 547

Lookback period: 90 days for regular creditors, 1 year for insiders

The debtor is presumed insolvent during the 90 days before filing

Key defenses: ordinary course, contemporaneous exchange, subsequent new value

Recovered funds are distributed equally among unsecured creditors

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the trustee take back my mortgage payments?

Usually no. Regular, on-time mortgage payments are protected by the ordinary course of business defense. However, an unusually large payment (such as paying down principal) within the preference period could be recovered.

What is an insider preference?

An insider is a relative, business partner, or corporate officer/director. Payments to insiders within one year before filing (not just 90 days) can be recovered. This extended period prevents debtors from favoring family members and business associates.

Is there a minimum amount for preference recovery?

For consumer debtors, aggregate transfers of less than $7,575 to a single creditor are protected from preference recovery. For business debtors, the threshold is $7,575 for non-consumer debts. These amounts are adjusted periodically.

Related Terms

Avoidance Action
Case Trustee
Bankruptcy Estate
Adversary Proceeding

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Priority Claim in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/priority-claim.html

What Is Priority Claim in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Priority Claim

A priority claim is a debt that receives special treatment in bankruptcy and must be paid before general unsecured creditors. Priority claims include domestic support obligations, administrative expenses, certain wages owed to employees, and specified tax obligations. In Chapter 13, all priority claims must be paid in full.

How It Works

Priority claims are ranked in order by 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a). The highest priority goes to domestic support obligations, followed by administrative expenses (trustee fees, attorney fees, costs of preserving the estate), then gap claims in involuntary cases, then employee wages (up to $15,150), then employee benefit plan contributions, and then specified tax claims.

In Chapter 7 liquidation, estate funds are distributed according to the priority order. Each level must be paid in full before any distribution to the next level. If funds are insufficient to pay an entire priority level, distribution within that level is pro rata. General unsecured creditors receive distribution only after all priority claims are satisfied.

In Chapter 13, all priority claims must be paid in full through the plan under Section 1322(a)(2). This is a mandatory requirement for confirmation. The debtor cannot propose a plan that pays priority claims less than 100% unless the creditor agrees to different treatment.

Key Facts

Ranked in order by 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a) - 10 priority levels

Domestic support obligations hold the highest priority

Must be paid in full in Chapter 13 as a condition of confirmation

Administrative expenses (trustee and attorney fees) are second priority

Priority taxes are nondischargeable - they survive even if not fully paid

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Priority Claims

Frequently Asked Questions

Are all taxes priority claims?

No. Only certain taxes qualify for priority status: income taxes where the return was due within 3 years, trust fund taxes (payroll taxes), and taxes assessed within 240 days. Older taxes may be general unsecured and dischargeable.

What are administrative expenses?

Administrative expenses are costs incurred in administering the bankruptcy estate: trustee commissions, attorney fees for the estate, accounting fees, and costs of preserving and liquidating estate property. They have second priority after domestic support obligations.

Do priority claims have to be paid in Chapter 7?

In Chapter 7, priority claims are paid from estate funds in order of priority. If there are insufficient funds (as in most no-asset cases), priority claims are not paid from the estate, but nondischargeable priority debts (taxes, support) still survive the discharge.

Related Terms

Domestic Support Obligation
Claim
Chapter 13
Unsecured Claim

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Proof of Claim in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/proof-of-claim.html

What Is Proof of Claim in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Proof of Claim

A proof of claim is a written statement filed by a creditor asserting the right to receive a distribution from the bankruptcy estate. It includes the amount owed, the basis for the claim, and supporting documentation such as account statements, contracts, or invoices.

How It Works

Creditors file proofs of claim using Official Form 410 with the bankruptcy court. The claim must include the creditor's name and address, the amount owed, the basis for the claim, and whether it is secured, priority, or unsecured. Supporting documentation must be attached.

The bar date - the deadline for filing proofs of claim - is set by the court. In Chapter 7 cases, the bar date is typically 70 days after the 341 meeting. In Chapter 13 cases, government claims have 180 days from the petition date, while non-government claims typically have 70 days from the 341 meeting.

Once filed, a proof of claim is deemed allowed unless the debtor, trustee, or another party in interest objects. Objections to claims can challenge the amount, the validity of the debt, the secured status, or the timeliness of the filing. The court resolves disputes at a claims hearing.

Key Facts

Filed on Official Form 410 with supporting documentation

Bar dates are strictly enforced - late claims may be disallowed

In Chapter 13, the debtor can file claims on behalf of creditors

Claims are deemed allowed unless objected to

Not required in Chapter 7 no-asset cases (no distribution)

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Proof of Claim Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if a creditor files a wrong amount?

You can file an objection to the claim, providing evidence of the correct amount. The court will schedule a hearing to resolve the dispute. Common errors include duplicate charges, wrong interest calculations, and inclusion of post-petition charges.

Can I file a claim for a creditor in Chapter 13?

Yes. Under Section 501(c) and Bankruptcy Rule 3004, the debtor can file a proof of claim on behalf of a creditor if the creditor fails to do so. This is useful when you want to ensure a creditor is paid through your plan.

What if a creditor misses the bar date?

Late claims are generally disallowed. The creditor loses the right to receive a distribution from the estate. In Chapter 13, some courts allow late claims under limited circumstances, but this varies by jurisdiction.

Related Terms

Claim
Secured Claim
Unsecured Claim
341 Meeting

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Reaffirmation Agreement in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/reaffirmation-agreement.html

What Is Reaffirmation Agreement in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Reaffirmation Agreement

A reaffirmation agreement is a legally binding contract between the debtor and a creditor in which the debtor agrees to remain personally liable for a specific debt despite the bankruptcy discharge. They are most commonly used to keep a vehicle, allowing the debtor to continue making payments and retain the car.

How It Works

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 524(c), a debtor can reaffirm a debt by entering into a written agreement with the creditor before the discharge is entered. The agreement must disclose the amount of the debt, the interest rate, and a comparison of the reaffirmation to the debtor's budget. The debtor has 60 days after filing the agreement to rescind it.

If the debtor is represented by an attorney, the attorney must certify that the reaffirmation does not impose an undue hardship and that the debtor was fully advised. If the debtor is not represented, or if the debtor's budget shows a negative cash flow, the court must hold a hearing and determine whether the reaffirmation is in the debtor's best interest.

Reaffirmation carries significant risk: if the debtor later defaults on the reaffirmed debt, the creditor can pursue collection on the full balance as if the bankruptcy never happened. The debtor loses the protection of the discharge for that specific debt. For this reason, many bankruptcy attorneys advise against reaffirmation when the debtor is underwater on the loan.

Key Facts

Governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 524(c) and (d)

Must be filed before the discharge order is entered

The debtor can rescind within 60 days of filing the agreement

Attorney must certify no undue hardship if debtor is represented

If debtor defaults, full collection rights are restored as if no bankruptcy occurred

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Reaffirmation Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I have to reaffirm my car loan?

No. Many debtors choose to keep paying without reaffirming (called 'retain and pay' or 'ride through'). Some lenders will continue reporting payments; others will not. Some circuits require debtors to choose: reaffirm, redeem, or surrender.

What happens if I reaffirm and then cannot pay?

The creditor can repossess the vehicle and sue you for the deficiency balance. You lose the bankruptcy discharge protection for that debt. This is the primary risk of reaffirmation.

Can I reaffirm a credit card?

Technically yes, but this is almost never advisable. Credit card debt is unsecured and dischargeable. Reaffirming it gives up the benefit of the discharge without any corresponding benefit to the debtor.

Related Terms

Discharge
Automatic Stay
Secured Claim
Chapter 7

Browse all glossary terms →

Check your bankruptcy discharge eligibility with our free screening tool.

Free Discharge Screener

## What Is Redemption in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/redemption.html

What Is Redemption in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Redemption

Redemption in bankruptcy allows a Chapter 7 debtor to keep secured personal property by paying the creditor the current fair market value of the collateral in a single lump sum payment, even if the amount owed on the loan is higher. It is an alternative to reaffirmation or surrender.

How It Works

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 722, an individual Chapter 7 debtor can redeem tangible personal property (not real estate) that is intended for personal, family, or household use by paying the secured creditor the replacement value of the property. This is typically much less than the outstanding loan balance.

For example, if a debtor owes $12,000 on a car worth $7,000, redemption allows the debtor to pay $7,000 (the car's value) and keep the vehicle. The remaining $5,000 is treated as unsecured debt and discharged. However, the payment must be made in a single lump sum, which is the main obstacle.

Because few debtors have thousands of dollars in cash available during bankruptcy, several lenders specialize in redemption financing - making loans specifically to fund redemption payments. These loans typically carry high interest rates (15-25%) but can still be advantageous when the vehicle is significantly underwater.

Key Facts

Available only in Chapter 7 for personal property (not real estate)

Debtor pays the current value of the collateral, not the full loan balance

Payment must be made in a single lump sum

Redemption financing is available from specialty lenders

The remaining loan balance above value is discharged as unsecured debt

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Redemption Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I redeem my house?

No. Section 722 redemption applies only to tangible personal property intended for personal, family, or household use. Real estate cannot be redeemed under this section. Home retention in Chapter 7 requires reaffirmation or continued payment.

Where do I get the money for a lump sum payment?

Options include family loans, redemption financing companies (722 Redemption, Fresh Start Lending), savings, or tax refunds. Redemption financing carries high interest rates but can save thousands compared to the original loan balance.

Is redemption better than reaffirmation?

If you owe significantly more than the vehicle is worth, redemption is usually better - you pay the lower value rather than the full loan balance. If you are close to equity, reaffirmation may be more practical since you avoid the lump sum requirement.

Related Terms

Reaffirmation Agreement
Secured Claim
Chapter 7
Lien

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Schedules in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/schedules.html

What Is Schedules in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Schedules

Bankruptcy schedules are the official forms that list the debtor's complete financial picture - all assets (Schedules A/B), exemptions claimed (Schedule C), secured creditors (Schedule D), unsecured priority creditors (Schedule E/F), unsecured nonpriority creditors (Schedule E/F), executory contracts (Schedule G), co-debtors (Schedule H), income (Schedule I), and expenses (Schedule J).

How It Works

The schedules must be filed with the bankruptcy petition or within 14 days of a bare petition filing. They provide the trustee, creditors, and the court with a complete snapshot of the debtor's financial life. Accuracy is critical - the schedules are filed under penalty of perjury and form the basis for the trustee's administration of the case.

Schedule A/B lists all property the debtor owns or has an interest in. Schedule C claims exemptions to protect listed property. Schedule D lists secured creditors (mortgages, car loans). Schedule E/F lists priority creditors (taxes, support obligations) and general unsecured creditors (credit cards, medical bills). Schedule I and J show current monthly income and expenses.

Errors or omissions in the schedules must be corrected by amendment. Failure to disclose assets can result in denial of discharge, revocation of discharge, or criminal prosecution for bankruptcy fraud. The schedules are public records and can be accessed through PACER.

Key Facts

Filed under penalty of perjury - accuracy is mandatory

Must be filed with the petition or within 14 days of a bare petition

Public records accessible through PACER

Errors must be corrected by amendment

Intentional omissions can result in denial of discharge or criminal prosecution

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Bankruptcy Schedules

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if I forget to list a creditor?

In most Chapter 7 no-asset cases, the omitted debt is still discharged. However, if the case is an asset case or a creditor needed notice to file a timely objection to discharge, the debt may survive. Always amend to add omitted creditors.

How do I value my property on the schedules?

Use replacement value - what it would cost to buy the item in its current condition from a retail source. For vehicles, use NADA or KBB private party value. For real estate, use a recent appraisal or tax assessment. The trustee may challenge valuations that appear too low.

Are my schedules public?

Yes. Bankruptcy schedules are public records filed with the federal court and available through PACER. Your Social Security number is partially redacted, but your name, address, assets, debts, and financial information are accessible to anyone.

Related Terms

Bankruptcy Petition
Statement of Financial Affairs
Exempt Property
341 Meeting

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Secured Claim in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/secured-claim.html

What Is Secured Claim in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Secured Claim

A secured claim is a creditor's claim that is backed by a lien on the debtor's property (collateral). The secured portion of the claim equals the value of the collateral or the amount of the debt, whichever is less. Common secured claims include mortgages, car loans, and home equity lines of credit.

How It Works

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 506(a), a claim is secured to the extent of the value of the collateral. If a creditor is owed $20,000 and the collateral is worth $15,000, the claim is bifurcated: $15,000 is a secured claim and $5,000 is an unsecured claim. This bifurcation is the basis for cram down in Chapter 13.

Secured creditors have significant rights in bankruptcy. The automatic stay prevents them from repossessing, but they can seek relief from the stay if not adequately protected. In Chapter 7, the debtor must choose to reaffirm, redeem, or surrender secured property. In Chapter 13, secured claims can be paid through the plan.

The interest rate on a secured claim in Chapter 13 is determined by the court using the 'prime plus' approach from Till v. SCS Credit Corp. (2004). The court starts with the prime rate and adds a risk factor, typically 1-3%. The debtor pays the secured claim amount plus this interest rate over the life of the plan.

Key Facts

Defined by 11 U.S.C. Section 506(a) - secured to the value of the collateral

Claims exceeding collateral value are bifurcated: secured + unsecured portions

Secured creditors can seek relief from the automatic stay

In Chapter 7: reaffirm, redeem, or surrender

In Chapter 13: paid through the plan at court-determined interest rate

Frequently Asked Questions

What if my car is worth less than I owe?

The claim is bifurcated under Section 506(a). The secured claim equals the car's value, and the excess is an unsecured claim. In Chapter 13, you may be able to cram down the loan to the car's value (if the loan is more than 910 days old).

Does my mortgage become unsecured if I am underwater?

No. Mortgages on the debtor's principal residence are protected from modification by Section 1322(b)(2). However, a wholly unsecured second mortgage can be stripped in Chapter 13.

What interest rate does a secured claim earn in Chapter 13?

The court sets the rate using the Till formula: prime rate plus a risk adjustment (usually 1-3%). This is typically lower than the original contract rate.

Related Terms

Lien
Cram Down
Unsecured Claim
Adequate Protection

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Serial Filer in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/serial-filer.html

What Is Serial Filer in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Serial Filer

A serial filer is a debtor who files multiple bankruptcy cases within a short period, often to repeatedly invoke the automatic stay to delay creditors. Serial filers face increasingly severe consequences: a limited 30-day stay on the second filing within a year, and potentially no stay at all on the third filing.

How It Works

BAPCPA addressed serial filing abuse through Section 362(c)(3) and (c)(4). If a debtor files a second case within one year after a prior case was dismissed, the automatic stay expires after 30 days unless the debtor proves the new filing is in good faith. If a debtor files a third (or subsequent) case within one year after two or more dismissed cases, no automatic stay takes effect at all.

Serial filing also affects discharge eligibility. Under Section 727(a)(8) and (9), debtors must wait specific periods between discharge-eligible filings: 8 years between Chapter 7 discharges, 6 years between a Chapter 13 and Chapter 7, 4 years between a Chapter 7 and Chapter 13, and 2 years between Chapter 13 discharges.

Courts scrutinize serial filers for good faith under Section 1325(a)(7) in Chapter 13 cases. A pattern of filing and dismissing cases without completing a plan raises a strong inference of bad faith and can lead to denial of confirmation, dismissal with a bar to refiling for 180 days, or even sanctions.

Key Facts

Second filing within 1 year: stay limited to 30 days (Section 362(c)(3))

Third filing within 1 year: no automatic stay at all (Section 362(c)(4))

Discharge timing limits: 8 years (Ch.7-Ch.7), 4 years (Ch.7-Ch.13), 2 years (Ch.13-Ch.13)

Courts can bar refiling for 180 days after dismissal

1328(f) governs repeat discharge eligibility in Chapter 13

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Discharge Screener

Frequently Asked Questions

How long do I have to wait to file again after dismissal?

There is no mandatory waiting period, but filing within one year of a dismissal limits your automatic stay to 30 days (or eliminates it entirely if two prior dismissals exist). Practically, waiting at least one year avoids these stay limitations.

Can I get a discharge in back-to-back cases?

Timing limits apply: 8 years between Chapter 7 discharges, 4 years from Chapter 7 to Chapter 13, 2 years between Chapter 13 discharges. If you file too soon, you will not receive a discharge even if you complete the case.

What is a Section 109(g) bar?

Section 109(g) bars a debtor from filing for 180 days if the prior case was dismissed for willful failure to obey court orders or was voluntarily dismissed after a creditor sought relief from the stay. This is an absolute bar - no exception.

Related Terms

Automatic Stay
Dismissal
Discharge
Good Faith

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Statement of Financial Affairs in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/statement-of-financial-affairs.html

What Is Statement of Financial Affairs in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Statement of Financial Affairs

The Statement of Financial Affairs (SOFA) is a required bankruptcy document that provides a detailed history of the debtor's financial transactions, lawsuits, property transfers, business interests, and other financial activities over the past several years. It is filed under penalty of perjury alongside the bankruptcy schedules.

How It Works

The SOFA (Official Form 107) asks approximately 30 questions about the debtor's recent financial history. Key questions cover: income from all sources for the current and prior two years, payments to creditors over $600 within 90 days (1 year for insiders), lawsuits the debtor was party to, property transfers within two years, gifts over $600, losses from fire/theft/gambling, and payments to attorneys.

The SOFA is one of the most important documents in the bankruptcy case. The trustee uses it to identify potential avoidance actions (preferences, fraudulent transfers), undisclosed assets, and potential grounds for denying discharge. Questions about payments to insiders and property transfers are particularly scrutinized.

Accuracy is essential. The SOFA is signed under penalty of perjury. Omissions or false statements can result in denial of discharge, revocation of a previously granted discharge, or criminal prosecution for bankruptcy fraud under 18 U.S.C. Section 152.

Key Facts

Official Form 107 - approximately 30 questions about financial history

Filed under penalty of perjury with the bankruptcy schedules

Covers payments, transfers, lawsuits, income, and business interests

The trustee uses it to identify preferences, fraudulent transfers, and fraud

False statements can result in criminal prosecution

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Filing Documents

Frequently Asked Questions

How far back does the SOFA look?

Most questions cover 1-2 years before filing. Income questions cover the current and prior 2 calendar years. Payment to creditors questions cover 90 days (1 year for insiders). Property transfer questions cover 2 years. Some questions (lawsuits, financial accounts) have longer lookback periods.

What if I cannot remember every payment?

Review bank statements, credit card records, and check registers to compile accurate answers. If you truly cannot determine a transaction, disclose what you know and note the uncertainty. Incomplete disclosure is always better than false or no disclosure.

Is the SOFA public?

Yes. Like all bankruptcy filings, the SOFA is a public record available through PACER. Financial information, payments to creditors, and lawsuit history are all visible to anyone who accesses the filing.

Related Terms

Schedules
Bankruptcy Petition
Preference
341 Meeting

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Stay Violation in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/stay-violation.html

What Is Stay Violation in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Stay Violation

A stay violation occurs when a creditor takes collection action against the debtor or the debtor's property after the automatic stay has taken effect. Stay violations can include phone calls, collection letters, lawsuits, foreclosures, repossessions, wage garnishments, and bank account freezes.

How It Works

The automatic stay under Section 362 prohibits virtually all collection activity from the moment the bankruptcy petition is filed. Any creditor who continues collection activity after the stay takes effect - even unknowingly - violates the stay. Willful violations under Section 362(k) entitle the debtor to actual damages, costs, attorney fees, and in some cases punitive damages.

Common stay violations include: a creditor filing a lawsuit after the bankruptcy was filed, continuing a garnishment, repossessing a vehicle, attempting foreclosure, calling or writing to collect a debt, offsetting a bank account, or reporting the debt as delinquent rather than 'included in bankruptcy' on credit reports.

The debtor can seek relief by filing a motion for contempt or a motion for damages under Section 362(k). The debtor must prove the creditor knew about the bankruptcy (had notice) and the action was willful - meaning the creditor intentionally performed the act, not that the creditor intended to violate the stay. Damages can include out-of-pocket costs, attorney fees, emotional distress, and punitive damages.

Key Facts

Governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 362(k)

Willful violations entitle the debtor to actual damages, costs, and attorney fees

The creditor must have had notice of the bankruptcy filing

'Willful' means the act was intentional - not that the creditor intended to violate the stay

Actions taken in violation of the stay are generally void or voidable

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Stay Violation Guide

Frequently Asked Questions

What should I do if a creditor violates the stay?

Document the violation (save letters, record dates of calls, take screenshots). Notify the creditor in writing that you have filed bankruptcy and provide the case number. If the violations continue, consult your attorney about filing a motion for contempt and damages.

Can I get money for a stay violation?

Yes. Under Section 362(k), you can recover actual damages (out-of-pocket costs, attorney fees) and in egregious cases, punitive damages. Some courts also award emotional distress damages for willful violations.

Are actions taken in violation of the stay valid?

Most courts hold that actions taken in violation of the automatic stay are void (have no legal effect) rather than voidable. This means a foreclosure sale or judgment entered in violation of the stay is automatically invalid.

Related Terms

Automatic Stay
Motion for Relief from Stay
Discharge Injunction
Bankruptcy Petition

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Substantial Abuse in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/substantial-abuse.html

What Is Substantial Abuse in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Substantial Abuse

Substantial abuse, now commonly referred to simply as 'abuse,' is the standard under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(b) for dismissing a Chapter 7 case when the debtor has the financial ability to repay a meaningful portion of their debts. BAPCPA replaced the 'substantial abuse' standard with a broader 'abuse' standard tied to the means test.

How It Works

Before BAPCPA (2005), Section 707(b) allowed dismissal only for 'substantial abuse' - a higher bar that gave debtors more latitude. BAPCPA lowered this to simply 'abuse' and introduced the means test as a mechanical way to identify abuse. If the debtor's means test shows sufficient disposable income, a presumption of abuse arises.

The presumption of abuse can be triggered in two ways: (1) the means test calculation on Form 122A-2 shows disposable income exceeding the statutory threshold (enough to pay at least 25% of general unsecured claims or $9,075 over 5 years), or (2) the totality of the debtor's financial circumstances shows the filing is an abuse of Chapter 7.

The debtor can rebut the presumption of abuse by showing 'special circumstances' - such as a serious medical condition, a call to active military duty, or other documented expenses that reduce disposable income below the threshold. The burden shifts to the debtor once the presumption arises.

Key Facts

BAPCPA (2005) changed 'substantial abuse' to 'abuse' - a lower bar for dismissal

The means test creates a mechanical presumption of abuse based on income

Abuse can also be found under the totality of circumstances (Section 707(b)(3))

The U.S. Trustee or court can raise the issue; creditors cannot in consumer cases with primarily consumer debts

Special circumstances can rebut the presumption (medical, military, etc.)

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Section 707(b) Abuse

Frequently Asked Questions

Who can raise the issue of abuse?

The U.S. Trustee, the case trustee, or the court can raise abuse sua sponte. In cases where consumer debts predominate, individual creditors generally cannot file a Section 707(b) motion.

What are 'special circumstances'?

Special circumstances are conditions that justify additional expenses or income adjustments not captured by the means test. Examples include serious medical conditions requiring ongoing treatment, mandatory military deployment, and caring for a chronically ill family member.

What happens if my case is dismissed for abuse?

The case is dismissed and your debts remain. You can file Chapter 13 instead, which allows repayment over 3-5 years. There is no waiting period to convert or refile under a different chapter, though the limited stay provisions may apply.

Related Terms

Means Test
Chapter 7
Dismissal
Disposable Income

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Trustee in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/trustee.html

What Is Trustee in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Trustee

A trustee in bankruptcy is an individual appointed to administer the bankruptcy estate. There are several types: Chapter 7 panel trustees who liquidate assets, Chapter 13 standing trustees who manage repayment plans, Chapter 11 trustees (appointed only for cause), and the U.S. Trustee who oversees the bankruptcy system.

How It Works

The U.S. Trustee Program, a component of the Department of Justice, appoints and supervises bankruptcy trustees. Chapter 7 panel trustees serve on a rotating basis and are assigned cases as they are filed. Chapter 13 standing trustees handle all Chapter 13 cases in their assigned division. Both are private individuals, not government employees.

The trustee's duties include: conducting the 341 meeting, examining the debtor's financial affairs, objecting to exemptions or discharge when appropriate, recovering avoidable transfers, liquidating non-exempt assets (Chapter 7), collecting and distributing plan payments (Chapter 13), and filing final reports with the court.

The U.S. Trustee plays a separate, supervisory role. The U.S. Trustee does not administer individual cases but oversees the system: appointing panel and standing trustees, monitoring case progress, filing abuse motions under Section 707(b), reviewing fee applications, and ensuring compliance with the Bankruptcy Code.

Key Facts

Chapter 7 panel trustees: assigned by rotation, liquidate non-exempt assets

Chapter 13 standing trustees: handle all cases in a division, manage plan payments

U.S. Trustee: DOJ component, oversees the bankruptcy system (not individual cases)

Trustees are compensated from estate funds (percentage-based)

A Chapter 11 trustee replaces the debtor in possession only for cause

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the trustee working for the creditors?

The trustee is a neutral fiduciary whose duty is to the estate and its creditors collectively. They do not represent any individual creditor but administer the case for the benefit of all parties according to the priorities established by the Bankruptcy Code.

How does the trustee get paid?

Chapter 7 trustees receive a $60 fee per no-asset case. In asset cases, they earn a percentage of distributions: 25% of the first $5,000, 10% of the next $45,000, 5% of the next $950,000, and 3% of amounts above $1,000,000. Chapter 13 trustees receive a percentage of plan payments (typically 7-10%).

Can I replace my trustee?

Not in the usual course. Trustees are assigned, not chosen. A trustee can be removed only for cause - misconduct, incompetence, or conflict of interest. This is extremely rare.

Related Terms

Case Trustee
341 Meeting
Bankruptcy Estate
Chapter 7

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Unsecured Claim in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/unsecured-claim.html

What Is Unsecured Claim in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Unsecured Claim

An unsecured claim is a creditor's right to payment that is not backed by collateral or a lien on the debtor's property. Common unsecured claims include credit card debt, medical bills, personal loans, and most lawsuit judgments. Unsecured creditors are last in line for payment and often receive little or nothing in bankruptcy.

How It Works

Unsecured claims are divided into two categories: priority unsecured claims and general unsecured claims. Priority claims (taxes, support obligations, wages) are paid first and in full. General unsecured claims are paid from whatever remains after secured and priority claims are satisfied.

In Chapter 7, general unsecured creditors receive a distribution only in asset cases - and even then, the distribution is often pennies on the dollar. In the approximately 95% of cases that are no-asset, unsecured creditors receive nothing. The remaining debt is discharged.

In Chapter 13, unsecured creditors receive whatever the debtor's disposable income can support over the 3-5 year plan, subject to the best interests test (at least as much as they would receive in Chapter 7). The percentage paid to unsecured creditors varies widely - from 0% to 100% - depending on the debtor's income and expenses.

Key Facts

Not backed by collateral - the creditor has no property to seize

General unsecured claims are lowest priority in distribution

In Chapter 7 no-asset cases, unsecured creditors receive nothing

In Chapter 13, payment ranges from 0% to 100% depending on disposable income

Most unsecured debt is dischargeable (credit cards, medical, personal loans)

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between secured and unsecured claims?

A secured claim is backed by collateral (a mortgage is secured by the house, a car loan by the vehicle). An unsecured claim has no collateral. If the debtor defaults on a secured debt, the creditor can seize the collateral. Unsecured creditors have no such right.

Will credit card companies get anything from my bankruptcy?

In most Chapter 7 cases, no. In Chapter 13, credit card companies receive whatever percentage the plan pays to general unsecured creditors. This can range from 0% to 100% depending on your disposable income and the best interests test.

Can unsecured debt become secured?

Yes, if the creditor obtains a judgment and records a judgment lien against the debtor's property. This is why timely bankruptcy filing can be important - filing before a creditor obtains a judgment lien keeps the debt unsecured and easier to discharge.

Related Terms

Secured Claim
Priority Claim
Claim
Discharge

Browse all glossary terms →

## What Is Voluntary Petition in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/voluntary-petition.html

What Is Voluntary Petition in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Voluntary Petition

A voluntary petition is a bankruptcy case initiated by the debtor, as opposed to an involuntary petition filed by creditors. The vast majority of bankruptcy cases - over 99% - are voluntary. The debtor chooses when to file, which chapter to file under, and which court to file in.

How It Works

Filing a voluntary petition is the first step in any self-initiated bankruptcy case. The debtor prepares the petition (Official Form 101), bankruptcy schedules, statement of financial affairs, means test form, and other required documents. The petition is filed with the clerk of the bankruptcy court in the district where the debtor has lived for the majority of the prior 180 days.

Before filing, the debtor must complete a credit counseling course from an approved provider within 180 days of filing. The certificate of completion must be filed with the petition. The debtor must also pay the filing fee ($338 for Chapter 7, $313 for Chapter 13) or file an application for installment payments or fee waiver.

The moment the voluntary petition is filed, three things happen: the automatic stay takes effect (stopping all collection activity), the bankruptcy estate is created (encompassing all of the debtor's property), and the case is assigned a number and trustee. Individual debtors can file singly or jointly with a spouse.

Key Facts

Over 99% of bankruptcy cases are voluntary - filed by the debtor

Requires pre-filing credit counseling certificate

Can be filed individually or jointly with a spouse

Triggers the automatic stay and creates the bankruptcy estate immediately

The debtor chooses the chapter (7, 11, 12, or 13)

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: How to File

Frequently Asked Questions

Can my spouse and I file together?

Yes. Married couples can file a joint voluntary petition, which creates a single bankruptcy estate and a single case. This is often more efficient and less expensive than filing two separate cases.

Where do I file?

You file in the federal bankruptcy court for the district where you have lived (or had your principal place of business) for the majority of the 180 days before filing. If you recently moved, you may need to file in your previous district.

Can I change chapters after filing?

Yes. You can convert a voluntary case from one chapter to another in most situations. For example, converting from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 if you can no longer make plan payments, or from Chapter 7 to Chapter 13 if you want to keep property the trustee would sell.

Related Terms

Involuntary Petition
Bankruptcy Petition
Automatic Stay
Filing Fee

## What Is Wildcard Exemption in Bankruptcy? | Definition and Guide
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/glossary/wildcard-exemption.html

What Is Wildcard Exemption in Bankruptcy?

Home › Glossary › Wildcard Exemption

The wildcard exemption allows a debtor to protect any type of property up to a specified dollar amount, regardless of the property's category. It is especially valuable for protecting assets that do not fit neatly into other exemption categories - cash, tax refunds, bank account balances, and miscellaneous personal property.

How It Works

The federal wildcard exemption under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d)(5) allows a debtor to exempt up to $1,475 of any property, plus up to $13,950 of any unused portion of the homestead exemption. This means a renter who does not use the homestead exemption can protect up to $15,425 in any property using the wildcard.

State wildcard exemptions vary significantly. Some states (like California's System 1, Missouri, and Ohio) offer generous wildcards of $5,000 or more. Other states offer no wildcard at all. The availability depends on whether the debtor's state allows the federal exemption choice and what the state's own wildcard provides.

The wildcard is often stacked with other exemptions. For example, a debtor might exempt a car under the motor vehicle exemption up to its limit, then apply wildcard dollars to protect additional equity in the same car. It can also protect assets that have no specific exemption category, like a coin collection, cryptocurrency, or money in a checking account.

Key Facts

Federal wildcard: $1,475 + up to $13,950 unused homestead = $15,425 max

Protects any type of property regardless of category

State wildcard amounts vary from $0 to $25,000+

Especially useful for renters who do not use a homestead exemption

Can be stacked with other specific exemptions

Related BTN Guide

For a deeper dive, see our dedicated guide: Exemptions by State

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use the wildcard on my car?

Yes. If your car's equity exceeds your state's motor vehicle exemption, you can apply wildcard dollars to protect the additional equity. This is a common strategy for keeping vehicles with moderate equity.

What if my state has no wildcard exemption?

If your state requires use of state exemptions and offers no wildcard, you are limited to the specific exemption categories your state provides. Some states compensate with generous specific exemptions even without a wildcard.

Can married couples double the wildcard?

In a joint filing, each spouse can claim their own set of exemptions. If the federal wildcard is available, a married couple could potentially protect up to $30,850 in any property using combined wildcards.

Related Terms

Exempt Property
Homestead Exemption
Bankruptcy Estate
Chapter 7

## What Happens When You File Bankruptcy? [2026]
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/

Skip to main content

What Happens When You File Bankruptcy?

Everything You Need to Know Before, During, and After

The Moment You File

The instant your bankruptcy petition is filed with the court, the automatic stay takes effect. Every creditor must stop all collection activity immediately - no more calls, no more lawsuits, no more garnishments, no more foreclosure proceedings. Learn about the automatic stay.

What You Keep

Bankruptcy does not take everything. Every state provides exemptions that protect essential property. In most cases you keep your home (especially in Chapter 13), your car (up to a value limit), retirement accounts (fully protected), personal belongings, and tools of your trade. Check your state's exemptions.

What Gets Discharged

Most unsecured debts are eliminated: credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, old utility bills, and most lawsuit judgments. Some debts survive bankruptcy: student loans (usually), recent taxes, child support, alimony, and debts from fraud. Non-dischargeable debts explained.

The 341 Meeting of Creditors

About 30 days after filing, you attend a brief hearing called the 341 meeting. The trustee asks questions about your finances under oath. Creditors may attend but rarely do. It typically takes 5-15 minutes. Complete 341 meeting guide.

Chapter 7 Timeline

Filing to discharge: approximately 4-6 months. Credit counseling (before filing) -> File petition -> Automatic stay -> 341 meeting (30 days) -> Discharge (60 days after 341) -> Case closed. What is Chapter 7?

Chapter 13 Timeline

Filing to discharge: 3-5 years (length of repayment plan). File petition -> Automatic stay -> 341 meeting -> Plan confirmation -> Monthly payments for 36-60 months -> Discharge. Chapter 13 plan guide.

Impact on Your Credit

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, most people see their credit score start recovering within 12-18 months of discharge. The fresh start eliminates the debt-to-income burden that was dragging your score down. Rebuilding credit after bankruptcy.

Life After Bankruptcy

You can get a car loan immediately (though at higher rates initially). FHA mortgage: 2 years after Chapter 7, 1 year into Chapter 13. New credit cards: often available within weeks of discharge (secured cards first). The stigma is largely a myth - millions of Americans file every year, including business owners, professionals, and families. Buying a house after bankruptcy.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will I lose my house?

Usually no. Chapter 13 is specifically designed to save homes from foreclosure. In Chapter 7, your homestead exemption protects equity up to a state-specified amount.

Will I lose my car?

In most cases, no. If you are current on payments and the equity is within your state's exemption, you keep it.

Can my employer fire me for filing bankruptcy?

No. Federal law (11 U.S.C. Section 525) prohibits discrimination by employers based on bankruptcy filing.

How soon can I buy a house after bankruptcy?

FHA loans are available 2 years after Chapter 7 discharge or 1 year into a Chapter 13 plan. Conventional loans typically require a 4-year wait.

Will bankruptcy stop wage garnishment?

Yes, immediately. The automatic stay halts all garnishment the moment you file.

## Privacy Policy - whathappensinbankruptcy.com
Source: https://whathappensinbankruptcy.com/privacy.html

whathappensinbankruptcy.com

Home
Privacy

Privacy Policy

How we handle your data. Short version: we don't sell it, share it, or use it for advertising.

Data We Collect

We use Google Analytics (GA4) to measure aggregate site traffic. This includes page views, session duration, approximate geographic region (country and city level), and device type. We do not collect names, email addresses, or personally identifiable information through analytics.

Aggregate event data from Google Analytics is also exported to Google BigQuery for research use. The BigQuery data is used only for internal trajectory analysis and network health reports, is not shared with third parties, and is not used for advertising.

What We Don't Do

We do not sell data. We do not run advertising. We do not collect financial information. We do not use retargeting. We do not share any user data with attorneys, law firms, creditors, debt collectors, or legal service providers.

Specifically, we do not enable Google Signals, Google Ads integration, User-ID collection, or any cross-device tracking feature in Google Analytics. GA4 operates in aggregate-traffic-measurement mode only on this site.

Cookies

We use only first-party cookies set by Google Analytics for aggregate traffic measurement. We do not use advertising cookies, tracking pixels, or third-party analytics cookies.

Third-Party Services

Google Analytics (GA4) - aggregate traffic measurement

Google BigQuery - aggregate event data warehouse for research use only; not shared, not used for advertising

Google Search Console - search query measurement (clicks, impressions, our own page rankings)

GitHub Pages - hosting

Contact Forms & Email

This site may link to contact forms or email addresses operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project. Any data you submit through those channels is handled under the Open Bankruptcy Project master privacy policy, which governs all sites in this network.

Children's Privacy

This site is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect information from children.

Data Retention

Analytics data is retained for 14 months per Google's standard retention settings. After that window, individual event data is automatically deleted by Google; aggregate report metrics remain available.

Your Rights

You may request deletion of any personal data we hold by contacting info@openbankruptcyproject.org. California residents have additional rights under CCPA. EU residents have additional rights under GDPR. All such requests are handled by the Open Bankruptcy Project.

Network Policy

This site is part of the Bankruptcy Transparency Network operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. The same privacy standards apply across every site in the network. The authoritative master policy is maintained at https://openbankruptcyproject.org/privacy.html.

Changes

We may update this policy from time to time. Changes are reflected on the master policy first and then mirrored across all network sites. Check the master policy for the most current version.

Effective: March 30, 2026  |  Updated: April 11, 2026
